speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43,1 seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that 21 footwear factories have closed their doors over the past 12 months, thereby causing the loss of some 2,500 jobs, while Canada is now faced with the highest unemployment rate in 37 years; and considering that the Canadian industry's share of the market is only 44 per cent, since imports have taken over 56 per cent of it, which causes a serious and damaging prejudice to the Canadian industry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford:
That the House urge the government to take immediate action to remedy the current situation by imposing quotas on imports, because of the serious crisis the Canadian industry is now facing.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ANALYSIS OF EMPLOYMENT PROSPECTS FOR YOUNG CANADIANS ENTERING LABOUR MARKET-MOTION UNDER S.O.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the recent Statistics Canada report on manpower supply trends for the Canadian labour force which predicts that employment prospects for many new labour force entrants with post-secondary education will not be good in the next 10 to 15 years, and since the trend is a national one, and in view of the fact that the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) expressed shock at this finding since he had told us in the House that the present new Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs for job creation are based upon an assumption that there will be general labour force shortages by 1980, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman):
That the Minister of Manpower and Immigration immediately set up a study by reputable labour economists to do a thorough analysis of the Canadian labour market on a continuing basis over the next year and a half, so that all high schools, colleges, technical institutes and universities, vocational and guidance directors and counsellors in Canada, will have some realistic ideas of the sectors in which employment prospects are going to be best for our young Canadian adults in the next decade.

speechtext:

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REDUCING RATE OF INCREASE TO TWO PER CENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would read again "An Energy Strategy for Canada, policies for self-reliance," which was issued one year ago, he would see that the target we set was to reduce the growth in energy consumption to 3.5 per cent or less. We made it clear in that report that we hoped to bring the figure down to an average of 2 per cent per year by 1990.
The report to which the hon. member referred, which is the basis of that statement contained in our energy strategy document, should be in my hands shortly. I have not yet seen it but have reason to believe, and have so stated many times, that with strict conservation methods, including many of those already announced, we should be able to reduce our growth in energy consumption to 2 per cent between the years 1985 and 1990.

I disagree, inasmuch as section 114 gives the Commission the authority to give out this information not only
Oral Questions
to its own employees but to any person providing it deems such a course advisable. My question to the minister is: are there any guidelines or regulations governing the conduct of the Commission with respect to distributing this highly confidential information?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I rise on a question of privilege which deals with a very important matter.
In a news bulletin broadcast by the CBC French network on Wednesday, May 11, 1977, Mr. Paul Racine, a journalist for that network, stated that according to information he had received from the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) five of our good Social Credit members were about to join the Liberal party; in other words, 50 per cent of the Social Credit caucus. Now, Mr. Speaker, such a statement on the part of a CBC journalist reporting the words of the Minister of Supply and Services deserves to be taken seriously, for it deals a blow to the reputation of each and every one of the Social

May 19, 1977
Oral Questions
Credit members in this House. Further to that statement, Mr. Speaker, I therefore want to dispel all the confusion it may have created in public minds: I have never had any intention of joining the Liberal ranks. I was elected under the banner of the Social Credit Party of Canada and the electors of Shefford have given me their trust as a Social Credit member. I must, however, confess that I did allow myself to be misled once, in 1956, when the Liberal party, to get the votes of the Socreds, included in its platform the following social credit principle: That all that is physically possible and morally good must be made financially achievable. Now, that statement from the minister, as reported on the CBC news by Mr. Paul Racine, was intended to discredit Socred members during the by-elections, while trying to create an atmosphere of confidence in the Quebec federal Liberals by spreading the rumor that members of all parties are about to join the Liberal party.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by dispelling any expectation the Liberal Party might have about me and I hope Radio-Canada is going to correct the impression it has created and will this time tell the truth instead of spreading mistakes and confusion which affect the credibility of individuals who are not all at the service of Radio-Canada or the Liberal Party.
Accordingly, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) tell the House the names of the five hon. members of the Social Credit Party who, according to him, are about to join the ranks of the Liberal Party, as he gave them to Mr. Paul Racine.

Obviously inadvertently, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources during the question period led the House and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands to believe that it is not the intention of the government at the present time to pursue the prospect of reprocessing nuclear waste for the purpose of extracting plutonium to double the efficiency of our reactors. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a matter of privilege concerning the answer given in this House today by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to the last
May 19, 1977

question I asked. At that time the minister left the impression in the House that other provinces of Canada had not indicated a willingness to participate in a national insulation program.
The reason I am suggesting the minister has misled the House is that the documents I relied upon in my question were documents tabled before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works yesterday, and those documents were also tabled at the energy ministers' conference on May 11. I would like to refer the House to the second page of that document which indicates that three provinces-British Columbia, Manitoba and Nova Scotia-have implemented a loans program. The federal government has contributed to the Nova Scotia program. Since that time, Ontario has indicated a loans program in a national insulation project. These provinces have clearly indicated their willingness to participate in a national program.
The Minister misled this House in saying that the provinces are not willing to undertake a national insulation program with the federal government. The minister can now proceed with the provinces of British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Ontario by simply providing federal grant funds for national insulation programs in those provinces, and we can begin next week on a national insulation program.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: GUIDELINES TO COMMISSION FOR DISTRIBUTION OF CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has exaggerated and distorted the situation out of all recognition. If he will look at the "blues", he will see I gave him an answer which indicated that if there was further evidence from the provinces that they were prepared to enter into programs of an insulation nature, I would like to receive it.
I am well aware of the initiatives taken by the province of British Columbia, the first province to do so through their public utilities. I have given them a great deal of recognition and have urged other provinces, other provincial utilities, other private utilities, other private companies and other commercial interests as well to follow the lead taken by the British Columbia government in this regard. That initiative on the part of the British Columbia government was not tied to a national insulation program in any way; it was done for their own purposes. In the case of Manitoba, I believe this was done for provincial reasons and it was not done from the point of view of its being a condition of a national insulation program. I applaud that initiative.
The most recent one the hon. member referred to is the province of Ontario. The announcements and the letters I have seen from the premier of the province indicate that the province of Ontario is going to introduce some kind of insulation loans program. It is not conditional in any way upon a national program or a grants program provided by the federal government. Quite clearly, these are loans programs being introduced by the provinces for their own purposes. They are sound initiatives, and I would urge other provinces to follow their lead. They are not conditional upon either a grants program or a national program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
That this House holds the Government directly responsible for the present economic disorder in Canada and the disastrous consequences of that disorder upon the spirit and unity of the country.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the debate which we are initiating is timely. It affords us an opportunity to deal once more with the problems confronting Canada at the present time and with the kind of direction which our country needs to come out unscathed and, let us hope, strengthened as a result of the serious crisis which it is now experiencing.
To become aware of the general dissatisfaction in Canada and the concern which is taxing at the utmost our collective energies, we only have to take note of the complaints voiced by the media and to add our personal observations. This is why if we wish to avoid the social disorders now afflicting other countries, we must make a collective effort of reflection and join in a common quest for remedies required under the circumstance. This debate is therefore an opportunity for us to undertake a constructive dialogue through which we could begin to fashion the new society of which we all dream.
However, being responsible for the direction of the country, the government must take special care to restore the economy and satisfy the legitimate political yearnings of various areas of the country. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the unrest felt in Canada

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
is due to a defective leadership in economic endeavours and a false conception of what the political leadership ought to be at the present time. The outstanding characteristic of that chaotic policy often arising from panic has been disproportion. No other government has so coldly and cruelly left so many workers unemployed.
There is no other example either of a government which, over a nine-year period, has allowed inflation to get out of control and has given it such a strong impetus by increasing during that period its own expenditures by more than 200 per cent. Even its most commendable initiatives have only met with a partial success. I am referring in particular to its policy on regional economic expansion of which the Economic Council of Canada was quite critical recently. I am sure the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) will forgive me for saying this, because I know that he, perhaps more than any other, knows that the 1968 act did not have the impact that everyone expected. Regional economic disparities remain unabated. It is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that in economic matters, the government has often started by building the roof instead of the foundations. The best example of this is perhaps the job-creation program.
Although it has its merits, no one can claim that ;t is an adequate answer to the chronic unemployment which affects so many Canadian regions and provides young Canadians especially with legitimate grievances.
I sincerely hope that Quebec City and Ottawa will play down their political differences and finally agree on a daring development program for the weakest or most promising industrial or regional sectors.
I take this opportunity to urge the government to deal most urgently with the critical situation in the Montreal building industry. Making Montreal a designated area, as it was two years ago, might relieve the unemployment situation, for some 40 per cent of construction workers in Greater Montreal are unemployed. I feel agreements in the areas of urban renewal, housing, water treatment plants and public transport system improvements are called for. They would certainly do more to revive the Montreal economy on a permanent basis than the construction of a giant complex such as Place Guy Favreau, as there is already in Montreal a plethora of office space.
We could discuss at length this problem of regional economic disparities and the government's inability to deal with it alone. The Economic Council of Canada, in the report 1 referred to a moment ago, rightly observed that the provinces were unduly left out of the implementation of programs designed to give a new impetus to their economy. It cannot be held against them when one of the main complaints of provincial governments is that they lack the financial means required to step up industrial development. Our long-standing tax system has too often compelled them to beg for federal funds. Such requests have resulted in delays and municipalities were the most heavily hit. Much delay would have been prevented if, in addition to a decentralization of taxation powers that has now become urgent, there had been between the federal and

provincial governments a body to coordinate their economic policies.
It was to such an agency that I was referring on February 21 last in this House, when I expressed the wish that an economic planning council be set up, or if you prefer, a national priorities council, to determine the joint undertakings of both levels of government in such sectors as industrial development.
Mr. Speaker, federalism cannot be judged solely on its economic profitability. However, every area of the country is still justified in wondering what benefits it derives from its participation in the Canadian confederation. Without relying blindly on figures and taking into account the intangible benefits of a social and especially political nature that the provinces derive from their belonging to a federated Canada, I hope that we will be better informed in the future about the economic aspects of Canadian federalism.
If only to enlighten those who run the country about the impact of certain measures on local economies, this type of study should be encouraged. If we were to discover that, indeed, such and such an area is unduly disdavantaged, it would then be possible to change our course without demanding, like the Pequistes, that the whole house be torn down because it needs repairs.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, that is the type of action that should be taken by the special unit set up recently in the Privy Council, supposedly to develop a strategy against the separatist movement in Quebec. We know very little about this group's terms of reference. For my part, I hope that it will not be content to find arguments against Quebec independance or to devise counter-tactics against the referendum. This agency should rise above mere controversy. It should undertake an in-depth study of Canadian federalism, in order to reveal its unquestionable merits, but without hiding its deficiencies or questionable orientations. I do not believe that the secrecy around the activities of this special unit is very healthy from a democratic standpoint. In fact, the government would be well-advised to refer its terms of reference to a parliamentary committee.
I would go even further. In this battle to save Confederation from the anguish of a break up, all supporters of federalism, no matter to which party they belong, should close ranks in a common strategy. The defence of the federative system is nobody's prerogative. This is why I suggest the creation of a parliamentary commission of members from all parties to diagnose the ills from which the present system may be suffering. This commission, which would be one of national conciliation and even reconciliation, could from the outset concentrate its efforts on identifying the causes of the national tensions. Having duly pin pointed them and considered the representations of the parties involved, the commission could submit a vast range of propositions arising from such representations and aimed at solving the difficulties about which we feel justified to complain. This first step would certainly be part of a long process which should eventually lead to the
May 19, 1977

constitutional reform whose necessity no one any longer denies.
That kind of political clearing house might make it possible to better determine what powers remain essential for the central government to keep the country together and what powers could be better exercised by the provinces so as to speed up the development of the various areas without jeopardizing Canada's federal nature.
As I said a moment ago in French, parliament should be associated more closely with the search for adequate solutions to the present national crisis.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
One way to do so would be to set up a parliamentary committee on a non-partisan basis. Its mandate at the start could be only to identify areas of conflict between the central and provincial governments and to deal in depth with their causes. Having done so, this committee could very well proceed further with substantive proposals of its own. In the meantime, this committee could very well examine the work being done by the special unit in the privy council dealing with the issue of national unity and about which very little is actually known by this House.

In that respect, Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that such a long time after the crisis started this government has not managed to make a greater contribution to the study and solution of the constitutional problem. I know that the Prime Minister will point to the Victoria Charter, but on second thought he will admit that it failed to meet all the claims not only of Quebec but of several, if not all, other Canadian provinces. It is all very well for the head of the government to say he is open to compromise and in the same breath express skepticism about the need for or the chances of success of such discussions. It is also very easy to build up an artificial popularity by denouncing Quebec separatists without considering why they advocate the secession of Quebec. Finally, it is very easy to claim that Canada is indivisible while too often, unfortunately, saying things that are likely to divide it even more. Such behaviour cannot protect Canada for long against the forces that would break it up.
It should be recognized, Mr. Speaker, that we, of the Progressive Conservative party, did not wait until November 15, 1976 to worry about the growing discontent in Quebec with the kind of federalism we have had for at least a decade. For at least a generation we have been cautioning Canadians against the dangers of en excessive centralization and we have in many areas proposed alternatives to alleviate tensions and bring about a better political balance in this country. If one really wants to be objective, it is obvious that our contribution to the constitutional dialogue is great and worthwhile, and that we have no lesson to take from anyone on Canadianism, quite the contrary.
Economic Situation

One should be careful, however, not to confuse, among reforms advocated by the Parti Quebecois, those which are specifically of a separatist nature and those which are also demanded by genuine federalist parties in Quebec. From Alexandre Taschereau in the thirties, for example, down to Rene Levesque, there has been a striking continuity of complaints about the way Canadian federalism has been implemented in such sensitive areas as social security and communications, to mention only those two issues. That the Parti Quebecois calls for complete separation in order to solve its differences with Ottawa does not necessarily mean that its grievances are without foundation and that they should be dismissed summarily. It is my hope and, indeed, my deep conviction, that at the forthcoming referendum Quebeckers will reject the separatist solution to their problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: But the yearning for a larger freedom of action at the political level will not die automatically. Ethnic groups naturally tend toward nationhood and statehood, and Quebec is no exception. The only way to avoid the final break-up of Canada in the future is for all of us to try hard to find ways of channelling the tremendous energies of the Quebec revolution into a new constitutional framework in which Quebec would more adequately assert herself culturally and economically.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
It is a fact that the Quebec premier's attitude is hardly better than that too often shown by the Prime Minister. Constant use of excessive language is no way to create between opponents a more sober climate, the lack of which might tear the country apart, and Quebec itself might never recover from that. Let Mr. Levesque prepare his referendum, since he has a mandate to do so, but let him remember in the meantime that as premier he is committed to respect the existing constitution.
Mr. Speaker, when 300,000 Quebecers are unemployed, when investments dwindle and nervousness takes hold of those who could help Quebec get on its feet again, the provincial premier has no excuse to take a rigid, dogmatic attitude which has no factual basis. Instead of behaving as if the people in Quebec had voted for independence, Premier Levesque would be better advised to use the tools at hand to restore a disquietly declining economy.
In addition, Mr. Levesque should stop fooling himself on the chances for a mutually agreeable separation. It takes a good deal of naivety to believe in pleasant divorces. If the Quebec premier persists in going his way in the face of Canadian hostility and international indifference, Quebecers will pay the price. And the price will be high in moral prestige, political influence and economic welfare.
5806

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
But it will not be enough for Canadians to counter separatism. We will have to learn the lesson and amend our political structures in such a way that each province, and especially Quebec, feels at home in a renovated federalism. In that respect, we should clear up a misunderstanding on which the Prime Minister has been relying too long in his attempt to counter secessionist forces in Quebec.
According to him, the general implementation at all political levels of the Official Languages Act alone would put an end to separatism in Quebec. This is a confusion between the aspirations of French Canada to cultural equality and those of French Quebec to political equality. However praiseworthy and necessary a bilingualism policy, it could not replace a constitutional reform. Only that reform is ever likely to conciliate the desire of French Quebec to become a separate political entity and its need to rely on federal structures able to extend its influence and to amplify its action. It is only under that condition that we will save Canada.
But in the meantime our two main linguistic communities must learn to live together and to develop freely in the mutual respect of their culture. Our history is such that our two founding people are united in blood and that modern Canada was born under the banner of war. It would be vain today to resume yesterday's fights in another form. I for one, Mr. Speaker, am prepared to forget the Plains of Abraham but in return I expect I shall not be reminded of them every day.
This is why, when the issue of minorities is more acute than ever, all Canadians of good will should find the answer in the fairness of a language policy and the fraternity of collective relationships.
To do this, we should consider drafting a charter of minorities that would define the linguistic and the educational rights of the English and the French elements of Canada. Time has come to proclaim A mari usque ad mare the equality of our two main national linguistic communities. Time has come to assert that local communities issued from them have the right to live and develop freely under the protection of laws and to the extent permitted by an heterogeneous environment.
I am not thinking, Mr. Speaker, of a mere statement proclaiming the equality of both official languages and the right of the two funding people to obtain from the state the means to achieve it. This charter of minorities should proclaim the basic right of men to belong to the culture they want and the obligation for the administration to allow them to exercise this right without legal restraints or worries. But the achievement of this purpose, Mr. Speaker, is yet a long way ahead. I happen to wish some times that Canadians get rid of the words generosity, tolerance and understanding in their vocabulary and replace them by one term: acceptance. We shall have to do just that if ever we want our country to survive the disruptions which have too often shattered it. Either we shall decide to accept one another with every compromise that our living together requires, and then we shall see the prospect of a tranquil and great future for Canada; or we shall meanly deprive the other linguistic group of its place in the sun, and then the clouds will grow darker still and the storm will roar.

Please God that at the end of the road we shall not be carried away by a swirl in which the very name of Canada would be but a recollection haunting the conscience of those who would have destroyed it. However, I prefer to conclude on an optimistic note. The years to come will certainly be difficult, our public men will have to act with wisdom and judgment and to show firmness to cope with the dangers which jeopardize our country and to funnel off, for the benefit of an innovating federalism, the centrifugal forces which threaten its unity. But our political leaders will be unable to save this country from collapse if Canadians themselves have not enough will to solve their problems in harmony, dignity and equality. They are the ones who, finally, will tell us whether the Canadian adventure is finished or if, on the contrary, revitalized by its experiences, Canada will start again its progress through history and will bear witness to the political genius and the spirit of brotherhood which inspire its citizens.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). I congratulate him on his lyricism, passion and concern for this country: it is just the tone of debate that is required in this serious matter facing our society. I wish to respond to the suggestion he put forward about a parliamentary committee, on a nonpartisan basis, to look into the causes of dissatisfaction in confederation. Those are not his exact words, but I think that was their intent. My party has discussed this matter but we have not reached a conclusion on it. I know the government has discussed it. I am trying to be nice. Usually, I have something other than nice to say. I am just trying to be nice and I hope they will accept that as a compliment. I am sure

that my leader, Mr. Broadbent, would approve the position they are taking, as would Mr. Lewis, Mr. Douglas, who is here, and as would M. J. Coldwell.

speechtext: Order, please. 1 suggest that the hon. member should refer to members of this House by their constituencies and not by their personal names.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Some do not have personal constituencies any more, so I took a liberty. I apologize for having used their personal names. In the other place, Senator Hazen Argue, if I may use that name, would even have approved of what has been said today.
This debate has been going on for years. It is not a recent debate; it has been going on as long as I can recall, certainly in my readings of the debates of the Commons long before I came here. Concern has always been expressed about holding the country together. It has been one of the cornerstones of Canadian policy. The great question asked by every government when it introduces a policy or takes a position is: What will it do to national unity? Therefore, it is not a new concern. It is a concern that has been around for a long time-the great confederation debate.
Years ago we took the position, I think the correct position, that while culture, language, and people wanting to determine their own lifestyle is important, it is as important that there be prosperity in Quebec as there be in the rest of Canada. We argued. It was called the class argument. There was a great deal of merit in that argument. We said that we cannot keep this country together if we have unemployment, if one part of the country feels that confederation is not giving it an economic break.
Many of the problems we face today in confederation, while not exclusively for this reason, arise directly from the fact that this government and governments before it have not been able to solve the economic difficulties created by unemployment. Unless these difficulties are solved, we are not going to solve the problems of confederation. That is what I was referring to as the lesson that hon. friends on my right have learned from the NDP. We have argued this matter over and over again. I cannot remember a time when we did not take that position. We now see that position being accepted.
It is interesting to look at the timing of the argument put forward in the motion today. Over the last week the Toronto Star has been running a series of articles on Quebec in which they have been exploring the psyche of Quebec to find out what it is that Quebec really wants. Is it language? Is it culture? The outstanding conclusion of what has been a very important survey is that economics are important in Quebec, unemployment is an important factor, and our ability as a federal government to solve the problems of unemployment may be the decisive issue as to whether we can hold this country together. Therefore, if my party talks about solutions which are not laissez-faire, which call for great government intervention and sticking out our necks, it is important that we pay attention to those solutions. There is no easy way of holding the country together.
Economic Situation
I want to say something in fairness to the government. I acknowledge that it is not going to be an easy problem to solve. The situation we face today has not been caused entirely by this administration or any particular administration before it. I do not think the problem would have been completely solved had the NDP been the government in Canada. A lot of this has to do with people's attitudes and their perception of our society. To the extent that Liberals and Conservatives have formed the government, it says something of the Canadian perception of their problems and the kinds of solutions they want to those problems. Our society-not only in Canada, but western society-is changing in a very dramatic way. All the evidence that we have before us, such as the studies carried out and the projections made, indicate a number of things.
If we continue on the path that we are going with our laissez-faire, tinkering attitude, unemployment will get worse. We think it is bad now. There are predictions by reliable people who can bolster their predictions with very sound arguments that the situation will get worse. I do not say it has to be worse; I simply say that if we proceed in the way we are, and do not do anything more than we are now doing-which is not very much-unemployment will increase in the future and confederation will be far from secure.
I wish to read a quotation in order to bolster what I am saying. I know that most members would take my word, but for those inclined not to do so I will read a bit of corroborating detail. I quote from an article which appeared in the Executive magazine of April, 1977:
Work is going to be hard to get for longer than most people have dared to imagine, unless there are some radical changes in work trends.
The very fact that a magazine like Executive would not edit out a word like "radical" indicates that they are a little concerned these days.
The most optimistic forecast I can make for 1986 is an unemployment rate of 11 per cent, and the worst case-also, unhappily, the most convincing case-is half as much again, around 17 per cent, or almost as bad as the unemployment Canada experienced at the height of the depression in 1933.
There are reasons for this. I am sorry I do not have as much time as I should like to have today to go into those regions. One of them is the falling birth rate. It is very significant. If you look at the past you will find that much of our growth and prosperity has been fuelled by the birthrate. It has been fuelled by cheap energy and cheap food. It has been fuelled because we did not care about the environment; we wrecked the environment and we despoiled, in one generation, what had not been despoiled for years. That cannot go on any more. It simply means that growth is not going to take place in the traditional way and that employment, as a consequence, will not be available in the traditional way.
Let me read from another article which deals with the question of growth in the foreseeable future. The article is entitled "The Growth of Growth" written by Leon C. Martel, executive vice-president and director of the research management council of the Hudson Institute. It is from "Futures", volume 9, No. 2. Might I, as a digression, put in a good word
80016-27%

Economic Situation
for the library clipping service? Those of us who use that service are grateful for the fact that they cull these articles, the kind of reading we are just not in a position to do, and make them available to us so we can keep in touch with some of the fine thinking which is going on not only in this country but internationally. Let me read from this article. These are excerpts, because of the shortage of time. The point of the article is to make the case that we cannot really count on the kind of automatic growth which has characterized not only our own society but the western world generally since the end of the Second World War. He says:
With insurance, social security and welfare for all, there will be protection against most of the vagaries of life, and this should produce a shift in priorities and values.
I should say at this point that while I have been critical of other parties, all of us, even with the best intentions, contribute to the kind of difficulty we are in. On balance, however, I would say that were it not for the welfare state, things would be much worse than they are. The welfare state itself creates problems, and that is one of the things we are facing. Some of the problems we have arise from the kind of security we build into the system. On the other hand-and this is far more important, in my opinion-were it not for the welfare system we have built in our society we would be in a worse depression than that experienced in the thirties.
Whatever abuses there may be with respect to unemployment insurance, without unemployment insurance, old age pensions, without medicare or hospital insurance, the western world would be in chaos right now. Having said that, we still have to recognize that this change in our society has itself created problems which call for new approaches and new ideas. The article goes on:
While the flower children of the 1960s have faded, the fact remains that a change in values has occurred.
This is a fundamental fact of our times. We are living in a different world, and the old solutions do not apply. They will not solve things. I continue quoting the article:
With mature economic development and the wealth it brings to individuals, there seems to be an increasing desire to leave things as they are, to be satisfied with the status quo. There is a growing emphasis on the protection and preservation of what one has, on health, comfort, safety, and the environment. This in turn spawns attitudes of risk aversion and localism.
In the past, in most cultures, people were taught that happiness was to be achieved as a more or less reasonable by-product of some other activity-a satisfactory job, the recognition of one's achievements, a devoted family, close friends, and so forth. Happiness was not usually recognized itself as an important value. However, today in affluent societies there is increasing emphasis on the direct search for happiness. The result is often a heedless hedonism.
The above trends and tendencies, and others which arise from them, can be found in varying degrees in most developed nations today. As they continue accelerating and reinforcing each other they will slow rates of growth. Already the process is under way and it is unlikely that Western Europe and North America will again experience sustained growth rates at the average annual level achieved in the decades following the Second World War.
Those of us who are close to the people of Canada, because we represent them, know this to be true. Our own personal experience tells us that our world has changed. While it may not be possible at this time fully to understand what we are going through or the way in which the change is taking place,

or the rate at which change is taking place, how many of us can say we do not sense the new society which is emerging or that we do not recognize that the old solutions are not working?
To get back to the central theme, the problem of unemployment and its effect on confederation, I want to say that while I give colleagues on my right high marks for learning their lesson today, I am not prepared to give them a full diploma, because while they have learned something from the NDP, it is only part of what we are saying. We are saying something else, and we have said it since the inception of our party. It is truer and more needed today than ever before.
What we are saying is that there is need for equal dignity for all. It will not be enough to provide jobs in Quebec, say, if they are ditch-digging jobs. This is what Quebec is saying and perhaps it is at the heart of the whole problem over language. Unfortunately, in Quebec language and jobs are related. It is an unfortunate fact that the big, important jobs were reserved for those who spoke English.
No self-respecting person can accept that in order to get a decent job he or she must learn somebody else's language. English, to Francophones, is somebody else's language. They are as entitled to their language as are the English. I should not have to state this, but I wish to do so to make clear what I am saying. This became obvious during the air controllers' strike. We talk about opportunity. Again, it is not enough to say we are going to create many jobs. What kind of jobs; and who is to get them? Will they be good jobs? I am sure that during the air controllers' strike a few months ago the question of air safety was an important one and that many of the people who put forward arguments on this basis were doing so with great sincerity. I do not question their motives. But in the way in which it was put forward, it was perceived as a means of preventing those who spoke French from getting jobs to which they were entitled. It was perceived as a way in which the English could continue to occupy positions at the top, to the detriment of the Francophones. Therefore, it is not enough to provide jobs. You have to ask about the quality of the jobs and the nature of the jobs, and there has to be equal dignity attached to them.
Then there is another matter. We have always talked about the need to redistribute income in this country, not only as between the English and the English but between the French and the English and perhaps between Canadians and the rest of the world. That is essential. If new jobs are created, some people will get very good jobs and others will get not such good jobs, and the gap between them will be enormous. Even if the question of language or the question of culture did not arise, we must see that these other matters are taken into account.
As it turns out, according to my calculations, in order to deal with this new world which all of us sense is upon us, and in order to deal with the new problems which are associated with this new world, we must redistribute income. We cannot go on having the disparity of income that exists in our society
May 19, 1977

today. Let me give an example of one incredible distortion which has taken place and for which we are to blame. If people are angry at their legislators for this, then I do not blame them. We encourage people to go to university. To learn, to enlarge their knowledge of the world? No-because university is the passport to making more money. We had the Dennison report, a study we copied from the United States, which related productivity and high income to education. Therefore, we falsely encouraged-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and through you may I thank my colleagues in the House. I appreciate this opportunity to continue for a few moments, but I will not be too long. This is an important point to me. Looking back, it is a terrible mistake which we made. We should have seen it, but most of us did not. Why did these people go to university? Because it was an "Open sesame". At a time when we needed plumbers, carpenters, machinists, orderlies, all kinds of people with practical skills we encouraged most of our students to get a B.A.
What has been the consequence of this? We are not the only country which has done this sort of thing. Every western country has done the same. We now have people coming out of university faced with fantastic frustration, knowing they have given four or five years of their lives to learn a skill for which there is no opening. They are resentful and bitter. It is hard to say to them "Yes, I know you have a B.A. in political science, but you may have to work side by side in a factory with someone who was a high school dropout".
In some ways we should not feel too bad about this, because having gone to school is not a waste. Anyone who has spent some time at school, whether or not they can apply everything they learned there, has done something to improve himself. If they have to work and get their hands dirty, so what? I do not buy the argument that because someone has a baccalaureate he has the right to go around with clean finger-nails for the rest of his life. We really have to demonstrate that we have respect for labour. We must make sure that a man who leaves home at five or six o'clock in the morning to go to work in a factory has equal treatment and equal pay with the person who leaves for the office at nine o'clock and perhaps returns home at four and never get his hands dirty.
We have had this double standard in our society, this cruel elitism, this aversion toward the blue-collar worker. We are now paying for it. We have forced a whole generation into believing that the road to dignity is the clean shirt. The road to dignity is more than just a clean shirt; it is what that person is and what kind of contribution that person makes. The waitress, the man who works in the factory or the orderly who works in the hospital deserve our praise and recognition, as
Economic Situation
does the lawyer, the doctor or the MP. We are entering upon a society where equality of income will no longer be some kind of socialist pipe dream where we pat a person on his head and say he is a fine fellow. That is very idealistic, but it will not work. What I am saying is that if that sort of thing happens then our society is not going to work.
There are other matters I should like to deal with, but I do not want to trespass upon the generosity of my colleagues who have granted me extra time. I want to conclude by pointing out some of the things which I think need to be done, aside from the general proposition I have been putting forward about redistribution of income and commitment to full employment. Our society must commit itself to work, not welfare. Welfare must certainly be provided if we cannot provide jobs, but it is a sign of our failure. If a person is receiving welfare or unemployment insurance because he cannot find a job, then that is not his fault. But we can certainly condemn a society that cannot solve the problem of providing jobs for its people. As I have said, we have to assert the dignity of all work; we have to get rid of elitism.
There are many things we can do, Mr. Speaker. We can embark upon capital projects, and to get the money for these we have to learn to tax those who have it. I know the House has been averse to doing this. The government, supported by the official opposition, had done the worst possible thing, faced with the kind of situation we are in. The last budget was essentially a budget which gave more to the well-off than it gave to the poor. At a time when we have to increase purchasing power and when our number one problem is unemployment, the government, supported by the official opposition, encourages savings. This is a good way to put ourselves into an even worse situation.

We should also give consideration to earlier retirement. Many young people have come to me and told me that their father or their uncle is working, that he is tired and they wish they could get a job. The uncle or the father, on the other hand, would probably say, "Why should I slug it out? Having worked 45 years, I should like to quit now". I say, let the young people have a job. Certainly, this is one of the changes the government must consider. I know this cannot be done in one fell swoop, but let the government at least work toward lowering the age of retirment. If it cannot be done for both men and women, then let us forget about women's lib and let us start to lower the age of retirement for women.
If the government does not want to do it on a universal basis, then let it be optional. But let us at least move in that direction since jobs will not be available for everyone. Just as we must create jobs, we must also take people off the labour market. If a person does not want to come off the labour market, fine. If a man wants to work until he is 80, I say good luck to him. But a lot of people do not want to do that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate at this point the mover of this motion on such an important, essential and urgent matter. We, in the House of Commons, are probably those who, in the history of this country, will have made the most momentous decision.
Therefore, 1 commend the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) for trying to bring serenity to a debate which could easily become overheated. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that it is very difficult to remain calm when the government resorts to arrogance, anger and sometimes even blackmail. I say Canadian problems will not be solved in a dispassionate manner as long as we have this government and particularly its leader.
Mr. Speaker, we must accept matters as they are. And when the future of the country lies in the hands of a sophist who is primarily interested in winning an intellectual argument, we cannot expect to solve our economical problems. It is quite normal also when we realize that the leaders of this country were so shortsighted that a few weeks prior to November 15, they were proclaiming all over the world, in Japan particularly, that there were no more separatists in Quebec. What are these people doing, Mr. Speaker? What are they doing now at the head of this country? I say that they are destroying it. And when I hear those same individuals accusing Quebecers in particular of trying to break Canada, Mr. Speaker, I say the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet have a real tunnel vision as to what Canadian unity means. They are now obsessed with their own idea of national unity and God knows that is not the answer for this country. We will have to come down to earth, as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe suggested, and realize that we have to create a climate where we can sit down and discuss, and agree on the best way to achieve Canadian unity.
And why would such unity not be achieved within a common market within which fully independent Canadian entities could develop freely? Why not, Mr. Speaker? Why has it to be this heavy burden of unpopular, costly, harmless bilingualism that the Prime Minister has been trying to establish for years when a majority of Canadians are against it? Mr. Speaker, this is a lack of realism. It is an attempt by someone to destroy the country with his fallacies. He is supported by irresponsible people who cheer him on, such as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) who is faced with the following dilemma: he wonders to what extent he should help Quebec, because in doing so, he proves that the Quebec government is right, and to what extent he should not restrain his department's expenditures and let Quebecers know that they had better stay within this obsolete and outmoded federalism which divides us.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, on the pretext of being too busy, refuses to meet the Quebec minister Mr. Leonard to finalize a federal-provincial agreement, which shows the goodwill of the Quebec government, when, instead of solving this problem, the minister prefers to campaign for the Liberal candidate in the Temiscamingue riding, I say that he is irresponsible, and this is what causes an unhealthy climate to develop, one which will bring about the destruction of this country. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that for those reasons I have to agree entirely with Rene Levesque who said lately about this minister, and I quote:
At present, they are a bunch of bunglers. That is how they behave! Mr. Macdonald went to New York to meet financial analysts and he told them the same old story of uncertainty, and so on.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, and I am no longer quoting, the Prime Minister went to Washington and he dared say a terrible thing-that if Quebec wanted to become independent, to develop freely in its own way, to come to an agreement with the rest of Canada in the best interests of the whole country, it would be a crime against mankind! Does our Prime Minister think he is God himself, Mr. Speaker, to say such nonsense and such terrible things? Well, such are the things which destroy this country. It is not the Quebec separatists only who want to compel Canada to find its own identity.
Mr. Speaker, this partnership that could be created among Canadians of goodwill, this true partnership based upon the absolute respect of sovereignty and the mutual agreements which could cover all the jurisdictions over those areas that can be administered in a comprehensive way, this is, I suggest, a very commendable goal, one which all of us in this House should try to achieve. This is also why you have Rene Matte, the member for Champlain, who fights for the independence of Quebec, but at the same time is prepared to discuss with everybody this country's future. This is easy to understand, there is no argument against it.
I would rather have a straightforward and honest proposal than pieces of sophistry, flip flops and what not, Mr. Speaker. One should see things as they are, and I go on quoting the Premier of Quebec:
As for me, I suggest that those people do not do their job as government members for the whole of Canada, which we are still part of, and within which we are quite willing to maintain normal relations which can be discussed among people representing the same kind and the same level of taxpayers. They are increasingly behaving like a bunch of petty terrorists. It seems to me that the majority of Quebecers should realize that. They do not behave as Quebecers and, in a way, at the national level, as good Canadians.
This is the attitude of the Prime Minister and his ministers when they try in every possible way to create a climate of uncertainty by making Quebecers fear their livelihood and their economic future is threatened. They say to them: "Go ahead, enroll in the fight for federalism." One thing must be realized, Mr. Speaker. At the time the men we would now call the "grand-daddies of Confederation" were holding their meetings, they had in mind some Unitarian form of government of course, but nothing like Confederation. This has been
May 19, 1977

the source of all sorts of problems, and this is why today we are at the turning point in our history. A solution must be found at all costs. But what is the governments doing? It is simply worsening the economic disorder. Therefore, the consequences of such disorder upon the spirit and unity of the country are disastrous, to quote from the motion.
Mr. Speaker, what is it that will prompt Quebecers to vote for independence at the next referendum? Why? The answer is: Because the people in an industry which has been basic in Quebec for years, as was the shoe industry, which used to supply 95 percent of the Canadian market 25 years ago, have seen that, thanks to the actions of the federal government, the total Canadian shoe production came down from 58.5 percent in 1968 to 51 percent in 1974, 50.7 percent in 1975, 45.8 percent in in 1976 and 32 per cent 1977. During that period, imports rose from 41.5 to 68 percent. That industry was mainly based in Quebec. Did the federal government help Quebecers keep their industry and increase their economic power? Not at all. People are wearing shoes from Sweden, from Taiwan, from Japan and Poland, but in the meantime Quebecers are unemployed. Is there a belief this will lead Quebecers to vote for federalism? Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec farmers producing 60 percent of the overall dairy production in Canada will vote for federalism, when the government has been systematically allowing increasing volumes of butter and cheese imports over the last ten years? Recently still, there could be seen in Quebec powdered milk bags from New Zealand, while the industrial milk producer was penalized because of powdered milk surpluses. Is that what a federal government is all about? Will Quebecers vote for Mr. Trudeau's kind of federalism? An end should be put to the monstrosities and historical absurdities we are hearing. Even when uttered from the Capitol in Washington, they do not become any more intelligent.
I think it would be better if the Prime Minister tried to cope with financial problems. Had nobody made suggestions we could understand that he has to look for them, but heaven knows our party particularly came up with proposals to settle that economic problem so as to pave the way for our country's unity, but I say a unity which would faithfully reflect the Canadian reality.
Mr. Speaker, we have noted all these things but then we see the government behave in such a way as to prompt businessmen like Mr. Crump, former Canadian Pacific chairman, to state the same sort of nonsense as the leader of the government, and I quote:
I believe that if this bill. ..
... speaking about the language bill in Quebec.
... is approved in its present form, any national or multinational company which will not move its head office from Quebec-will do its owners a disservice.
Mr. Speaker, why did Mr. Crump say that? That is what the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) has been telling us for weeks, he who has been seeing head offices heading for the nearest border. He is creating that artificial atmosphere, which is why the economic situation is so disastrous. So I will conclude by saying that it is absolutely
Economic Situation
important, particularly in this place, that we should come down to earth and stop thinking ill-advisedly that Canadian unity has only one form. We should have open minds and be Canadians enough, I should say, to understand that perhaps the present Quebec government is the one which most wants Canada to continue as a nation, but that it should do so in full respect for its components.

speechtext:
I shall leave it to someone else. I think that such a contribution deserves only to be ignored in the debate we want to have today.
The motion blames the government for the economic disorder in Canada and deplores its consequences on the spirit and unity of the country. I thought we were going to discuss in length the economic situation but apparently they preferred to place the debate in a larger context and I do not object to this, on the contrary.
I would like to deal with a few points made by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) and make a few comments on some of his remarks. I am pleased to hear and note how his views are akin to the government's in a great many areas. As a matter of fact, some of his statements, and suggestions have been made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or some ministers on various occasions. Whether it is the matter of the Francophones' rights in this country, or the importance of guaranteeing the Francophone community not only linguistic but also economic rights and a fair economic role in keeping with their talents, those concerns are exactly those the government has been expressing for a number of years. As for revising our federalism, again this is nothing new, since in 1966 and 1967, this government brought about proposals for a complete review of the Canadian constitution.
Those discussions led to several premiers' conferences and to a proposal known as the Victoria Charter. For historical reasons that are well known, there was no agreement at that

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
time, but it is important to remember that in spite of those failures, over the years, the Prime Minister indicated to the provinces, again in a letter he sent them at the beginning of last December, that he was willing to sit down with them at any time and either discuss a restricted formula for amending the Constitution, in order to repatriate our Constitution, or to make a complete revision of our Constitution, depending on the choice and discretion of the provinces. Until now, most provinces have not seen fit to follow up that proposal. Some of them seem to have indicated they were considering it. Others, particularly Quebec, have repeatedly indicated that their government was not interested in any negotiation whatsoever before the referendum was held. Again last weekend, the premier of Quebec took that position.
It may also be important to recall what the Prime Minister said in this regard in Quebec City not so long ago because, to my mind, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe gave, in his speech, a truncated if not erroneous interpretation of the position of the government with regard to the whole matter. When we stand up for the French language, when we champion the equality of the two languages in this country, we do not do so as if it were the only means of frustrating the separatist tendencies evident in Quebec. The official languages proposal was put many years ago and once again, not for strictly political, immediate, or partisan objectives: it was made to guarantee the Francophones of this country, and the Anglophones as well where they are in a minority the rights to which they are entitled. It is merely a matter of respecting the minorities in Canada. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe spoke of a charter for the minorities: that is precisely what the government proposed in Victoria when it was suggested that a list of the fundamental rights of the citizens, and especially recognition of their linguistic rights, should be entrenched in the Canadian Constitution.
There again, even if there were absolutely no separatist tendencies in Canada, even if no one was trying to break up the country I am convinced, as well as this government, that it would have been necessary, in all fairness, to enact legislation such as the Official Languages Act which this Parliament adopted. But it is a far cry from that to claiming that the position of the government is based strictly on a linguistic matter, and that it is the opinion of the government that in meeting the linguistic problems we will solve all problems of a political nature in our country; this is surely a false and erroneous interpretation of the stand taken by this government. Moreover, I remind the House of the statement the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made in Quebec City quite recently, when he addressed the Quebec Board of Trade on January 31: He said quite clearly and I quote:
In the constitution, I think there is only one principle, that is to respect the rights of men and women, the respect of human rights, and probably the respect of the collective aspect of these human rights. I'm thinking of language, the right of regions to exist. And from this principle you can start from the beginning: write a new constitution. We haven't had one in 110 years, we can make one. And I refuse no challenge. All that I ask as long as I am here is that it must be concretely established that such and such a level of power, for example, must be exercised at the federal-provincial level in such a way that the Canadian community will profit by it.

This, Mr. Speaker, is the position of the Prime Minister, and of this government. We have indicated once again, as recently as in the letter the Prime Minister wrote in early December to the provinces, that we are always ready to sit down and discuss such a basic constitutional review.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious on the other hand that there is a fundamental disagreement between the position of this government and that of the Quebec government at this time. And never will my colleagues or myself subscribe to an objective aimed at the destruction of this country and the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada. However, this does not mean once again that we are for the constitutional status quo or that it is impossible to consider certain rearrangements of powers between the provincial governments and the federal government. The great flexibility of federalism, Mr. Speaker, has been demonstrated by the fact that there are not two identical federal systems in the whole world and that many forms of federalism can be found among the various countries that have adopted that form of government throughout the world. But when once again the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe suggests in his speech that his party has been concerned about over-centralization for years, he is truthfully stating the speeches made by his colleagues in recent years. But what is important to note is not so much the speeches on this matter, but the facts. And what are the facts? Well, the facts are that there is practically not a government in the world today or a country in the world with a federal form of government that has a system as decentralized as Canada. I will only mention, for example, the United States, Germany, Switzerland, Australia, where the central power accounts for a much greater part of the total public expenditures than the Canadian government today.
And this is borne out by the evolution of public expenditures in recent years. Mr. Speaker, suffice to recall that in 1965, after transfers to the provinces the federal government took 53 per cent of the tax base, and that percentage went to 40 per cent in 1975. And in 1977, under the agreement reached at the last conference of first ministers last December, it is expected that the percentage of the tax base accruing to the federal government will represent only 37 per cent as compared with 63 per cent going to the provinces and municipalities. Well, when the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe was suggesting in his speech that the provinces are complaining of a lack of funds to carry out industrial development, I think that is a somewhat limited perception of the situation. In fact, provinces and municipalities have taken an increasingly larger share of the tax basis and the question now being asked by many is whether the federal government will soon be left with a share of the tax basis large enough to be able to truly assume its responsibilities and keep its commitments.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe also talked about a national priority council. I would remind the House that we have had a national priority council in Canada for many years and that it takes various forms. It can be found within federal-provincial conferences, where ministers are commissioned by their government to decide to jointly agree on the
May 19, 1977

directions to be given to various areas of government activity. When there is a meeting of either the ministers of agriculture or the ministers of health and welfare, or the ministers of energy, or the finance ministers on a regular basis as we have seen, and finally, when the premiers meet as frequently and as regularly as has been the case in the last few years, on those occasions the provincial and federal governments do in fact sit down together and determine our national priorities, and these priorities are set by the people who are democratically responsible to their constituents for assuming the burden of the decisions which are made during these meetings.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe also talked about the need for better information on the economic aspects of federalism. I believe that all governments have become aware of this in the last few years and through the ministers of finance, considerable work has been done by federal-provincial committees on all economic aspects of the Canadian activity. To have considerable statistical information on the taxation situation and the economic situation of the various areas of the country is nothing new. In the last few years, Statistics Canada has made considerable efforts to improve the quality of information in this field so as to truly allow an informed debate among the citizens and the government in Canada to take place, and we are happy to see that more and more information is given to the public in this area.
Unfortunately, some people make reference to it abusively and in a partisan spirit. I am referring particularly to the famous economic accounts that the Quebec government made public recently and which, obviously, backfired on those who thought they had planted a bomb within the federal system. It is quite interesting to see how the Quebec government, and the ministers who were involved in this matter, are now shunning the subject and trying to ignore this sad experience.
I think that it might be a lesson to all those who should be careful not to put words into their mouths, not to distort them for purely sectarian reasons, and in so doing delude and mislead the public, which cannot promote a worthy and healthy democratic debate.
The mover of the motion has also regretted that the opposition seemed to be unaware of the work done by the national unity group. I remind him that the director of this group met with each party leader when the group was formed and he mentioned, on behalf of the government, that he was at the disposal of the party leaders and/or the parliamentary groups of each party and/or the party caucus, and that whenever these groups would like to meet him and have discussions, he would be ready to do so.
Finally, as to the proposal to establish a parliamentary committee that would look into the causes of the uneasiness in our country and would propose means of improving the situation in Canada, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe also knows that this is another question which has been explored by the parliamentary leaders of the various political parties, and we shall have to await the result of those discussions before making a final decision as to the timeliness of such action.
Economic Situation
In the few minutes I have left, I should like, Mr. Speaker, to deal with and put on record a number of facts pertaining to the very nature of the motion before us. That motion deals with the situation of the economy, and I think the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) was quite right when he said it was impossible to talk about the political situation in Canada without dealing with the economy, and that it was an illusion to think that Canadian federalism could work if the Canadian economy does not work.
Of course, in the last few years our country has faced and is still facing economic problems. The government is aware of it and is concerned about this situation, and it has taken various steps and measures in order to solve, at least in part, these problems, whether it be unemployment or inflation. Here I should like to quote what an old Franciscan friend of mine used to say: "When I look at myself, I grieve, but when I compare myself to others, I take heart." The same remark could apply to the Canadian economy.
A few days ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) tabled in the House the Economic Review for 1976. This review provides us with a most valuable reference work to assess the performance of the Candadian economy not in isolation but in the general context of the world economy. I regret that my colleague the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, an expert on international affairs, did not deal with this matter within a somewhat broader context.
I shall refer to the fact that 1976 was a year of continued economic recovery following the most severe slowdown in over 30 years. In most of the major member countries of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the OECD, the upturn happened in early 1975. In the OECD area, the real output increased at the annual rate of A'h per cent in the second half of 1975, and showed a 6 per cent rate in the first half of 1976. As personal expenditures stabilized and inventories became negligible, there was a 3'A per cent slowdown in the annual growth rate in the second half of 1976. The slow recovery was due to the fact that the authorities were cautious in stimulating demand, because of the underlying inflation, and to the fact that investments did not take over at the usual stage of expansion. For the whole year 1976, the real growth rate averaged 5 per cent in the OECD area. In the 24 OECD member countries, consumer prices, after an average increase of 11.4 per cent in 1975, showed an 8.6 per cent increase in 1976. With a 7.5 per cent rate, Canada ranked fourth for the slowest price increase, behind Switzerland, West Germany and the United States.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to a recent study prepared by the national bureau of economic research in the United States. The study showed that in comparison with the other six major western industrialized nations, Canada had the best economic recovery from the 1973-75 recession. This country's index of economic performance in March of this
5814

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
year, according to the bureau, was 67 per cent ahead of its situation at the start of that recession.
This reflects the fact that because of the economic policies pursued by this government in the early 1970's, the drop in Canadian economic activity was not nearly as severe as that experienced by other countries. Comparable figures for West Germany, France and the United States show that their recovery was not as strong. It was between 2 per cent and 10 per cent of their pre-recession situation. Italy, Japan and the United Kingdom, on the other hand, have not yet recovered fully the level of economic activity they experienced prior to the recession. This study, prepared in advance of the recent London summit meeting, is based on a monthly index of economic performance which summarizes in a single indicator the more important measures of aggregate economic activity such as income, output, employment, unemployment, and sales.
The authors of the study, which was published in the New York Times, note that reliance on any single measure of economic activity, even such important and frequently used indicators as the index of industrial production and the rate of unemployment, can give erroneous assessments of economic performance. To underscore the fact that persistent high levels of unemployment are an international phenomenon, the study reveals that none of the countries attending the Downing Street summit has yet managed to get its unemployment rate down to the levels prior to the recession.
May I remind the House that this particular subject was one of the topics discussed at the Economic Summit on May 7 and 8. Canada, together with the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan and Italy, took part in the Economic Summit in London. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) emphasized the critical importance of dealing in a systematic and co-ordinated way with the economic problems facing the western world. This approach was welcomed by all the leaders present and provided the basis for the Downing Street declaration which was issued following the summit conference. I would like to quote a few sentences from that declaration because they summarize the approach being taken by Canada and our western allies to solve the economic challenges before us. I quote:
The world economy has to be seen as a whole; it involves not only co-operation among national government but also strengthening appropriate international organizations. We were reinforced in our awareness of the interrelationship of all the issues before us, as well as our interdependence. We are determined to respond collectively to the challenges of the future.
Our most urgent task is to create more jobs while continuing to reduce inflation. Inflation does not reduce unemployment. On the contrary, it is one of its major causes. We are particularly concerned about the problem of unemployment among young people.
We commit our governments to stated economic growth targets or to stabilization policies which, taken as whole, should provide a basis for sustained non-inflationary growth.
We will provide strong political leadership to expand opportunities for trade to strengthen the open international trading system, which will increase job oppor-

tunities. We reject protectionism: it would foster unemployment, increase inflation and undermine the welfare of our peoples.
The message of the Downing Street Summit is thus one of confidence:
-in the continuing strength of our societies and proven democratic principles that give them vitality;
-that we are undertaking the measures needed to overcome problems and achieve a more prosperous future.
This is the statement to which Canada subscribed. Canada was a very, very active participant indeed in the preparation of this statement.

We share those objectives with the other industrialized countries that participated in the London summit meeting. We want to reach those objectives in close co-operation with those countries. We also want to reach those objectives through the measures we are going to take and implement in Canada. And much as we must get the co-operation of other industrialized countries, so must we get the close co-operation of all provincial governments in this country with the federal government. Our work will be all the more easier if we can depend on that close co-operation and avoid a partisan approach to the economic debates.
Earlier the hon. member for Champlain mentioned my colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). Obviously, Mr. Speaker, ministers cannot be at the disposal of another minister on a six- or ten-hour notice each time they receive a telegram. But for the infomation of the hon. member I shall tell him that my colleague is meeting with the Quebec Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and they are having discussions aimed at improving the existing agreements. And I hope that that new spirit of co-operation rather than confrontation shown by that Quebec colleague will reflect on several of his other colleagues as concerns economic development in Quebec, particularly during the coming months and years.
We are not looking for confrontation or conflicts. We have the responsibility to work for the economic advancement of all regions of the country and since November 15, all my colleagues have constantly consulted the economic communities in Canada and abroad to encourage investors to continue their investments in Quebec and Canada during the months and years to come. When the Quebec premier recently made statements comparable to those of the hon. member for Champlain in this House, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) was perfectly right to say that the premier "perdait les pedales" as we say in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, those are the brief comments I wanted to make on the important issue raised by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. I thank the House for its good attention and I hope that the contributions to this debate will be on a par with those of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe and of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge.
May 19, 1977
