subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is often said that "plus 5a change, plus c'est la meme chose". To begin with this afternoon, I would like to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I think there was not too much partisanship, which shows that my colleague's motion deals with a fundamental problem in this country, quite a debatable motion actually in this House in the way we should have debates and discussions here in the House. This is Parliament, Mr. Speaker, where we express our views. We exchange them eventually. Since we come from various parts of the country, accommodations can be made and it is in accommodation that lies the success of our federation. After all, it is the lesson given during the last century by all federations. They represent various interests, but undoubtedly they realize, and that is indisputable, that the strength of the federation far exceeds the individual strengths of federation members, but once in a while, problems do arise.

I would like to go back almost a century, to 1878, when the first Liberal prime minister, Alexander Mackenzie, observed that there were three great problems facing Canada at that time: inflation, unemployment, and national unity. Of course. Canada was only 11 years old then. It was not a thrust that came out of Quebec or out of what was formerly Lower Canada which called national unity into question. It was from Nova Scotia. If one bothers to read Canadian history, a subject which is not taught very much in our schools and one
Economic Situation
in which present-day commentators are not well versed, one recalls that Joseph Howe actually got the Nova Scotia legislature to pass a resolution approving withdrawal from confederation. But such was the good sense of the people of Nova Scotia that they saw this was not the right way. So the little firecrackers we now hear, banging off here and there in certain areas of Canada, not only in Quebec-there are some damp squibs which go off from time to time in western Canada-are nothing new.
[DOT] (nio)
There is one further dimension. Today we are seeing far too much confrontation, a sort of dialectic approach to the problem which to my mind contributes nothing to an eventual solution. Some have suggested that our feelings on this question are more tense than they were years ago. Well, Mr. Speaker, I don't know. If we read the important speeches of Joseph Howe and the others of his generation, I am sure we would be persuaded that Canadians of a century ago spoke with as much heat and emotion as people do today. It is true, of course, that this could be appreciated directly only by those who listened to them at political meetings, or, to a lesser extent, read their speeches as reported in the press; there were no facilities for instant communication such as we have today, nor for the almost equally instant editorializing which is done by program producers with regard to the comments of today's political leaders as they appear on radio or television. Nevertheless, I suggest the intensity of emotion was just as great in those days as it is now.
Perhaps our problems are more complex. I do not know whether this is true or not. Complexity is always relative. As to the solutions which might be proposed, in their context they will not be more dramatic. They will certainly not be more untried than those put forward by the pioneers of this country. I do not look upon this motion as being a matter of Canada versus Quebec, or of Quebec versus the rest.

Or of French-speaking Canadians, not only in Quebec but elsewhere, versus the rest of the country. Not at all. What is the text of this motion? I quote:
That this House holds the Government directly responsible for the present economic disorder ...
It is about economic disorder. We must consider this matter and unfortunately the minister did not go through the question. I think that he evaded this difficulty wisely and carefully because we know that there is economic disorder throughout Canada. And the motion concluded this way, and I quote:
... and the disastrous consequences of that disorder upon the spirit and unity of the country.

Of course, the economic problems of the country must be reflected in the attitudes of Canadians wherever they may live, and they certainly are applying strains on national unity. The media maintain a high profile for the situation in Quebec. But that is only a symptom of the malaise which has existed all along in confederation. The people of Quebec express them-

selves culturally, linguistically and in other ways because they are a people and they have been affected by regional circumstances. There is no such thing as painting Canada with the same brush from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria. Commentators have always thought in terms of finding a sudden solution to Canada's problems.
Mr. Speaker, we shall always have problems. We have had them for a hundred years. We have them today. We shall have them a century from now, perhaps because there are so many factors over which man has no control, including the fact that he cannot be relied upon always to make the best decision. Let us see where we can go to fight this regionalism. Economic difficulties? We have had inflation since 1968 under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I remember seeing him before the television cameras announcing measures of stringency, restrictions on the hiring of new public servants, and so forth. I happened to be enjoying a holiday on Cape Breton Island on that occasion. I was in Sydney, Nova Scotia, that day and I watched the Prime Minister telling us the government had resolved to deal with inflation. It was not very long afterwards that he told us inflation had been wrestled to the ground. But it continued. Some 18 months ago the then minister of finance quarrelled with his prime minister, resigned and slammed the door. They talk about splits in parties! What was that but a split, and a fundamental split?
We have had inflation, and it is the federal government which is responsible for allowing it to develop and to carry through from 1968 to 1975 relatively unchecked. As a matter of fact, in the early 1970s they were in there fuelling it with the greatest of coal shovels, piling on the heat. We have had nothing but a history of accelerating unemployment. The solutions have been shoved under the carpet. Here and there there has been a mandate, but no fundamental solutions. Or if there were solutions to be applied, the government has failed right across the country to recognize the problems on a regional basis.
We have declining exports on a constant dollar basis. Our trade is in one hell of a mess. We are faced with high cost and low productivity. In what I am saying now I am going after hon. friends to my far left.

I do not want to create the impression that government is happy with the way today's economy is performing. I do not want to create the impression that the government does not realize the very things hon. members opposite have been saying-it is unemployment which is our most serious problem. Especially unemployment among the youth of Canada and unemployment in the depressed regions are problems. Our performance has been the best compared to the seven countries referred to in that study. What are the alternatives being proposed by hon. members opposite? I was interested in the comments of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte)-

-what the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) had to say. For him, it was the importation of goods at a lower cost than the cost of production in Canada!

Close the door and give Canadians a protective market for shoes? Let us make all our own shoes; let us make all our own electronic equipment? A lot of people in Canada see that as our salvation. Let me deal with one solution I have heard well-meaning people bring forward in my riding as 1 go around it defending and explaining the government's economic policy. People say to me, "Why was it possible for our economy to produce full employment during the war? No one was looking for a job during the war. We were able to place everybody in jobs, and could have placed even more people. Why cannot we return to that kind of economy? Our economy has worked well for us. We have begun to fall behind, begun to think that the $6, $7 and $8-an-hour-job can be found without harder work, without doing more and without creating more. It received its greatest push when international economies, including our own, were threatened with recession, which was more serious abroad but certainly serious in our own country. We reached the point at which we had to take dramatic action to protect our economy, to preserve the kind of economy which has been doing very well for us. Ours is a free enterprise, mixed type of economy.
What action did we take? We introduced the controls program, which has now been in effect for over a year. Our
Economic Situation
experience in the first year was good. We beat our target, even though lots of people did not think we would. We are taking advantage of the period of controls, of this pause, to make a number of fundamental changes.

Perhaps not. Increasing the money supply before the controls program was introduced had an important purpose. It tended to keep the interest rate lower, and it helped us not to fall into the kind of economic recession into which our neighbour to the south fell. In any event, during the controls period the rate of growth of the money supply has been brought down to a level the Conservative party must consider reasonable-although recently the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said in another place that the expansion is still too high. It is within the target figure which he said two years ago this government could not reach. That is the first thing that has happened during the control period.
The second thing that has happened is the restraint of growth of the federal government. This has been extremely important, not because there were not good reasons for the government service to grow previously, but because there were good reasons for the government rate of growth to slow down during the control period. I do not want to repeat the speeches which have been made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). It is a matter of record that important government restraint has been achieved during this control period, and a commitment has been made by this government to continue to honour restraint even after the controls come off

and to keep the growth in the 1977-78 fiscal year well within the growth of the gross national product.
What further has been done? A number of structural changes are under consideration. The competition bill is now before parliament. It will have the effect of making the economy more competitive in areas where market power is considered to be a problem. At the same time it recognizes that bigness is not necessarily bad, and that where bigness benefits the consumer, under the surveillance procedures provided in the bill it will be permitted to continue.
In addition, we are looking at industrial relations. A 14 point program has been put forward by th Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), aimed directly at improving industrial relations, the temperament of the workplace, the safety of the workplace, and relations between labour and management.
The structure of industrial relations is up for review. A number of proposals have been made. Some of them are so sensible one wonders why they were not implemented years ago. For example, a broader base for collective bargaining is being sought. Why should the total air industry go out on strike when the ticket sellers cannot settle their collective agreement? When the ticket sellers come to an agreement and go back to work and then when the pilots cannot settle their differences, why should the whole industry again go on strike? When the pilots settle their differences and go back to work and then when the air traffic controllers' negotiations break down, why should the whole industry go on strike again. Obviously the broader the base, the fewer days lost there will be within particular industries. I hope provincial ministers of labour will be looking at these proposals for reform in industrial relations. 1 hope that before the controls come off we will see important steps forward in improving this area of tremendous weakness in the Canadian economy.
We cannot simply follow the example of any other country. We have to find our own way, but we know we have to improve the mechanisms we have. An hon. member opposite asked what has been done. Well, a remarkable new rapport has been reached between two sectors which have always been in confrontation in Canada in the past. Labour and management are talking to each other during this period of controls in a way that they never have before talked. They are looking for a common position which they can put to the government which would provide a basis for removing the controls earlier than would otherwise be possible. They are taking some of the confrontation and hostility out of their relationship and hopefully making it possible for settlements to be reached in the future and for prices to be determined in a way which will not take us back to the kind of inflation we have had until now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I will not disappoint hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), by a lack of serenity in the remarks I am planning to make this evening. I may very well introduce a note of accerbity into this debate. I am indeed a bit bitter, but I am more angry than bitter.
May 19, 1977

On occasion we say in English that we speak more in sorrow than in anger. On this particular occasion I speak in sorrow and in anger because of the great disillusion that has been brought about for me, because of the fate that my country is now suffering as a result of the mismanagement by this government. I have always had a vision of Canada. Otherwise I would not have volunteered 36 or 37 years to be sure that that vision could be realized.
[ Translation]
I cannot conceal from you, Mr. Speaker, that I am worried and concerned over recent events, particularly the result of the vote taken last November 15 in the province of Quebec. The Liberal party is now ruthlessly campaigning to blame or to put the responsibility for the Liberal defeat by the electors of our neighbour province, on the CBC or on the English-speaking population of the rest of Canada. This campaigning will go on without respite, I am sure, until the by-election and maybe even until the general election. The Liberal party is looking for a scapegoat.
Those who are truly responsible, Mr. Speaker, first examine their own actions and their conscience. Right after a defeat or in an abnormal situation, they do not try to put the blame on others. On the contrary, they question themselves to find out where they made a mistake, where they went wrong. Let me indicate how 1 interpret the events of November 15: the population wanted to reject a government in which it has lost confidence, a reflection of the government in Ottawa, provincial and federal governments alike. And why has all confidence been lost in the federal government? Just look at the economic situation of the country! I would dearly love to read today's motion:

That this House holds the Government directly responsible for the present economic disorder in Canada and the disastrous consequences of that disorder upon the spirit and unity of the country.
[ Translation]
I support that motion wholeheartedly. Why have the people lost all confidence in the federal government? The economic situation is one explanation. It inspires no confidence in the direction taken by the government. Look also at the atmosphere of confrontation in which Pierre Trudeau's federal government governs. The Prime Minister has decided to govern, through federal-provincial confrontations, labour confrontations, cultural confrontations. That government preaches animosity. As for the respect we owe parliamentary institutions, for instance, one needs only look at the attitude of the present government in that regard.
Recently, to mention but one example, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), within 48 hours, made two statements outside the House of Commons concerning basic changes in railway and maritime transports in Canada. Those statements should have been made in the House, thus allowing hon. members to ask for details or express censure.
This government, Mr. Speaker, wants to govern without consulting the electorate or its representatives, the members of parliament. That is why, in my opinion, the role of Parliament
Economic Situation
is declining, and as a result the spirit and unity of the country are suffering, which partially explains the results of the vote of November 15. I feel a deep concern over the future of our country. That future will be seriously jeopardized if the role of Parliament is not restored. Our party, the Progressive Conservative party, which is the one that founded our country, is dedicated under the leadership of Mr. Clark to restoring the credibility of our parliamentary institutions by consulting Canadians regularly and thoroughly to identify their wishes. [English]
When I think in terms of my vision of Canada, 1 go back to a very famous speech. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to, not paraphrase, but alter the words to the present context. The speech was made more than a hundred years ago and it reads like this in its modern interpretation:
Five score years ago and more our forbears brought forth on this continent a nation dedicated to the proposition that two peoples of differing cultural and linguistic backgrounds could live in harmony together and thrive.
This is my Canada.
Less than five years later that notion was extended geographically from coast to coast, and a bare 20 years later a rail line connected one coast with another thus binding the country from sea to sea with bonds of steel. In less than 20 years a great miracle was accomplished with political and engineering ramifications of tremendous consequence.
Barely ten years ago we celebrated our centennial. That was the year of hope, jubilation and thanksgiving. What happened to the thrill of 1967, the high spirits and the expectation felt at that time? Just ten years later, where have they gone? Where did we go wrong? I submit we went wrong in 1968. We did not lose the way. We all have our vision of Canada and our dreams. The way was lost for us by this government. It was lost for us economically, constitutionally, and in parliament itself. It has been lost for us through the degradation of respect for law and the will to work. These last ten years have done untold damage to our country. I can do no more than sketch in some of the highlights.
In that period the national debt has doubled from $20 billion to more than $40 billion. The size of the public service has almost doubled. The budget increases are almost incredible. It is hard to believe that from a budget of $10 billion, more or less, in 1968, the budget has grown until, in 1977, it is $42 billion. It has quadrupled.
It is instructive to note the failure of the government in the economic field. In terms of promised growth, there has been under performance; in terms of exports, under performance; in terms of foreign direct investment, under performance. The figures are revealing. In 1971 direct foreign investment in Canada totalled $925 million. By 1975 it had fallen to $630 million. By 1976 foreign countries had reduced the value of their holdings by nearly $400 million showing their lack of confidence in this country.
As I have shown, there has been over-performance in government spending. A record job has been done on inflation.

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
There has been over-performance in areas which leave lasting, tell-tale marks on the economy, and under performance where it would count. In the area of employment opportunities there has been under performance. When it comes to providing proper incentives for investment, there has been under performance.
There is another element which concerns me greatly and it is one which has contributed to the disunity of this country and to the falling off in morale. It is the degradation of our institutions, including the institution in which we now speak. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made one speech in this House since October of last year, I think it was. His policy pronouncements are made either in another parliament in another country, in the Press Club across the road, or somewhere out in Saskatoon or elsewhere on the prairies, but not in this Chamber. He is totally lacking in regard for this place. His attitude is one of arrogance. Although not here at the time, I suppose I figure among those he has called nobodies. Members across the floor do not even recognize that they are nobodies, too, in his eyes. I have suggested that they come across to this side of the House and watch the Prime Mini ^er when he is performing. Hon. members over there see the back of his head. I see the disdain on his face. I have witnessed the profanity used by the Prime Minister in this House. It is true he said he regretted it, but what he regretted was that it got on the record. And when he was taxed about it he did not apologize. He just expressed regret and said he hoped he had not caused any inconvenience. And then, when the matter was picked up again he used even more unacceptable profanity.

I was proud to be elected to this Chamber in 1972 because I thought I was going to an institution which had a constructive role to play in the development of Canada. What did I find? I found in those four and a half years a government which has no regard for this institution and which has driven our country deeper and deeper into the morass. There are so many instances of abuse, misuse, and arrogance on the part of this government with respect to this House. One can cite the use of public transportation to transport domestic help to this country until it was brought to the attention of the public by the press; then it ceased. In fact the domestic help had to pay part of its way back.
Respect for law has also been downgraded as a result of the activities of this government. It in turn has had its adverse effect on morale and the desire for unity in this country. How can there be unity when this institution has been downgraded and no one respects it, because the government itself has no respect for it? That is our great problem. If we had a core in this parliament of ours which people in Canada respected, we would have a core around which to rally and we would have unity. It is the flight from that which has contributed enormously to the disunity which we are observing in this country today.

As for respect for law, Mr. Speaker, do you remember the judges who were telephoned? I remember one incident which never got on the record and I am determined to put it on the record now. It occurred on June 3, 1976, an interview of the Prime Minister by Gordon Henderson on the Global television network. This was at the time when the constitutionality of the AIB was being tested and the Prime Minister said that the Supreme Court would not decide the Anti-Inflation Act was unconstitutional. He then said, "Why do you ask that question?" The interviewer replied that that was the question that had been put to it, so the Prime Minister replied, "Well, I'm telling you what the Supreme Court is going to decide". The interviewer said; "You are confident then, Sir?" You could not guess the reply, Mr. Speaker. It was, "I phoned a few judges". Then there were titters and there was laughter. That is no laughing matter, Mr. Speaker. Even if it was said in jest it is no laughing matter to degrade, not just this institution but the Supreme Court of this country. It is absolutely incredible that that should happen, but since it has happened it is not so incredible that we should be suffering as we are from disunity and a sagging morale.
Another comment made by a minister which I feel cannot go unchallenged was this-I cannot remember the exact date-

He complained that French Canadians have been denied the opportunity to share in the development and shaping of Canada. That is not only mischievous, it is misleading, and is a monstrous distortion of history and the current situation. It just should not stand unchallenged. On hearing this I drew up a list of large corporate institutions, and 16 out of the first 50 of these largest institutions in Canada have their headquarters in the province of Quebec.
We all give due honour to our French speaking forebears who discovered the western regions of our country, whose names are remembered out there, some of whom were martyred. They were saints from that generation. All are revered. That comment by the Minister of National Health and Welfare deserves to go down in history, I think, as one of the most deplorable comments that could be made.
I have many, many other comments to make on this matter since I am deeply distressed at what the government has done to my country and the vision I had of my country. However, I do maintain it and I will go on doing my utmost to make sure that this vision will become a reality.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was preparing a few notes and thought I might come on a little later, but I am pleased indeed to enter into this debate and to make some remarks to my colleagues in the House is an attempt to bridge the two matters which are raised in the resolution before us, namely, economic policy and national unity. 1 am going to do so in the search for some perspective.
I am going to begin with the suggestion that all regions of Canada have such fundamental economic problems that they need each other in a new way, perhaps in a way they have not needed each other since Confederation; and that it is this convergence of need and difficulty which each region faces which gives us all the possibility of rebalancing Confederation at the level of economic structure and basic economic policy. I include Ontario in this description of the fundamental economic problems facing regions of Canada. I do so particularly because it is often assumed that Ontario has benefited the most from Confederation; that Ontario is so rich and strong that it is this province which is called upon to make concessions, to show some leadership, to concede certain things in order to hold the country together. What I want to fit into my remarks is the notion that Ontario too is in deep economic trouble and in relative industrial decline.
We can cope with this, but to do so Ontario needs all the other regions of Canada in striving for a new economic balance. This is one of the hopeful things which will bring about a new set of compromises suited to our needs, just as the compromises made at confederation established economic destinies, as it were, or vocations for the various regions of our country 110 years ago. This will therefore be is my thesis.
I am going to focus on the prairie provinces and suggest that the grievances of the prairie provinces can be regarded as frustrated industrialism. These grievances can be accommodated. Accommodating them would be more than simple justice for the prairie provinces. It would be more than fulfilment in the economic sense for prairie potentials. Accommodating those grievances would help solve Ontario's pending and present economic problems. Therefore there can be a basis for unity in industrial policy.
The grievances of the prairie provinces with respect to industrial policy come at the same time as Quebec's pre-occupation with language, culture, and a political sovereignty thought to be necessary to protect those objectives. In a sense, therefore, the confederation compromises are coming unstuck. What were they? In a broad sense, as expressed partly in the national policy of Sir John A. Macdonald, they may be summarized as this: in the central part of Canada there would be built a strong industrial heartland. My point is that that heartland is eroding and losing its strength in a relative sense. In the west there would be created a resources vocation. The prairie provinces would be filled up with immigrants and would be linked to the other regions of Canada via railway. The industrial heartland would be protected by a tariff system. The national railway network would be protected by moving
Economic Situation
goods behind that tariff barrier to the east and to the west, exchanging the products of each region.
The confederation compromises included for Quebec measures which were thought to be sufficient to protect cultural, linguistic, educational, and legal interests. Those are now being challenged as indequate. I will not say that they are being rejected. The prairie provinces are rejecting the vocation of a resources area which was laid out for them in the confederation compromises. Ontario by a series of economic development is no longer the confident secure industrial heartland. Transportation policy is challenged and tariffs are no longer significant to protect it.
I should like to review the evolution of the western economy to support my thesis. The western economy began with wheat. It is based on wheat, minerals, cattle, forests, oil and gas, all moved in bulk as basically raw materials with freight rates which reinforce that vocation for western Canada. They are freight rates which support the movement of raw materials as opposed to processed materials. The clearest example is rape-seed, and it is true in the sense of cattle as opposed to meat. Rapeseed moves to Vancouver and over to Japan at the Crowsnest Pass rates which are very low rates, indeed. They encourage the export of seed. Crushing takes place in Japan and employment takes place in Japan. In a sense those freight rates confirm the west as an exporter of raw materials. The movement of those products to eastern Canada is four or five times more expensive through the transportation system. This economic bias is frequently expressed in hostility to freight rates. What is being frustrated, however, is the further processing of the product in the prairie region. What is being frustrated is the value added, better jobs, higher incomes and more opportunities because the policy system locks the region into an earlier regional destiny.
The prairie provinces feel ready for the next stage of economic development which is further processing and industrialism. They are seeking not only a rearrangement of the transportation rates but a negotiation on tariffs in the United States. These negotiations must be carried on by Ottawa. The negotiations would seek to lower the rapid escalation of tariffs in the United States against the import of processed products. Look for example at the natural gas which is produced in Alberta. It can be exported without tariff to the United States. Ethylene, which is made from natural gas, can be exported without tariff. Ethylene is a building block in a long series of plastic industries and other industries. The United States will take that basic block without putting any tariff wall against it. If the west wishes to proceed to the next stage of industrialism, which would be polyethylene of considerably greater value in terms of incomes and balance of payments, it faces a 20 per cent tariff. If it went to the next derivative which is polyvinylchloride, the tariff would escalate again. How can industrialism come to the west if we do not negotiate downward the escalating tariffs of the United States? Thus, there is not only transportation. There are tariff negotiations and the question of assured markets in Canada for those processed products. One cannot build further processing based solely on exports.

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
What are we prepared to do in Central Canada to accept processed goods from the prairie provinces? Will we buy meat or will we not? We may buy it if we change the freight rates. Will we buy polyethylene, or will we insist on making it only in Sarnia? Ontario and Quebec therefore have a question to ask themselves with respect to national unity as reflected in the economic policy influencing prairie attitudes. They have to ask themselves whether they are prepared to see a different vocation for the prairie provinces than the one laid out 110 years ago, and reinforced by national policies over which we have control. I am thinking of assurances which may not be of the same kind, but in spirit they are similar to the assurances which were given to the western crude oil market in eastern Canada when it was a question of assuring the development of that industry. Assured markets went only to the crude oil stage. Are we now prepared to alter transportation and other mixes of policies so that industrialism can come to western Canada? If we are not, we are not working at the question of national unity reflected in basic economic policy.
Ontario is in such economic difficulty that it is perhaps prepared to look at that question in a new light. What are its economic difficulties? I do not want to speak in a gloomy way this evening, but there is cause for concern. We hear it said with validity that the central industrial heartland is no longer competitive with the products of the Third World and the United States, which is our principal market. For various reasons we have always been less productive in the sense of value of production per worker, value of production per man hour, and value of production per unit of capital employed.
However one measures productivity, it is generally accepted that Canadian manufacturing is about 20 per cent less productive than U.S. manufacturing. Not all our industries are less productive. Some are more productive. However, on average, it is true to say we are less productive. According to a Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce study which I have before me, our labour productivity is perhaps 18 per cent lower, as measured in 1972 terms. When one combines the productivity of labour with that of capital the picture becomes even worse. For example, according to figures for 1972, the rubber and plastics industry in Canada is almost 27 per cent less productive; the furniture industry 27 per cent less productive; knitting mills 32 per cent less productive; printing and publishing 41 per cent less productive, and so on. It is thus unfair to speak only of the differences in labour productivity, of our productivity levels being 18 per cent lower. When you combine labour with management, whose function it is to use capital and labour in efficient combinations you see that we are 38 per cent less productive on the average in the manufac-turiel section. Therefore one can see that there is a real problem in how we employ capital in this country and manage our industries.
Our wage costs are often higher than in the United States. Money used as capital costs Canadians between 15 per cent and 20 per cent more than it costs Americans. Construction

costs are higher in this country because of severe weather and other conditions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: And inadequate federal policies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
As one looks at the total picture, it becomes increasingly obvious that this so-called strong industrial heartland has entered a new phase of non-competitiveness and stready erosion. We have not yet felt the impact of manufactured goods produced in Third World countries. They will sweep over our remaining tariff barriers. In addition, we face non-tariff barriers in our best market. Those kinds of barriers have been erected to protect that market against products of the kind we will allow duty-free entry to Canada, because of our desire to help transfer economic resources to the Third World. Therefore the future of this industrial heartland of which I speak is not bright.
Why do I say that the future of this industrial heartland is tied to the future of western Canada? It seems to me Ontario needs an industrializing western Canada to which it can sell the products of its higher technology. Ontario needs an assured Canadian market for its higher technology products, exactly in the same way as it needed a somewhat assured market in the past to which to sell the products of its standard technology. We can only face foreign competition if we develop our higher technological capabilities; we can only develop these capabilities if there is a market to which we can sell the products of our higher technology. We cannot export all such products; we need a central economic base, or a market for them in this country. Surely an industrialized west will provide us with such a market. For example, it could use a control technology for processing. In exchange, we should accept the products which the west will want to sell to us. By so doing we would not only use our transport system efficiently but, by helping other regions, help to foster national unity. By all this I am suggesting that we need to examine again national economic policies. We must admit we are in deep trouble and need an industrialized west, as much as 100 years ago we needed the primary resources of western Canada.
I am emphasizing Ontario's difficulties, not because I wish to highlight our present difficulties, but because I wish to suggest that if Ontario understands where its own interests lie it will seek a new relationship with western Canada. Our best prospects for hope lie in western Canada. That is where a good deal of our industrial future lies.
I urge hon. members to examine what the Science Council has to say about technological sovereignty, for they will note some startling statements. For example, a summary of a paper presented at a seminar reads in part:
The paper presents the argument that Canadian secondary manufacturing is trapped in an evolutionary cul-de-sac. Past and extant policies have promoted modest industrialization along with technological underdevelopment and dependency.
The Science Council says that we are trapped partly because we are technologically dependent on others for innovation. Therefore, we must restructure industrial policies in Canada to
May 19, 1977

escape from this trap. I suggest we should look again at western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief, having already made my principal point. Let me continue speaking on industrial policy. It seems to me that we, at the political level, are again called on to make the sort of choice Sir John A. Macdonald made in this House 100 years ago. Perhaps we have depended too much on bureaucratic systems, depended on them to improve our economic performance. That course, I suggest, is no longer acceptable in this country. We need a new economic design, so to speak, rather than merely better performance under existing structures. But producing a new economic design is very difficult politically. It might mean choosing to help those industries in Canada which have some promise of life. We would have to specialize, and help to consolidate some industries. Perhaps government procurement policies would have to support those industries which promise to stay alive, and in trade we must stop acting as boy scouts. That is to say, Marshall support mainly for those industries which are critical for the success of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I did not dwell on the question of Quebec, serious though that is. I wanted to talk about economic policies in relation to unity. What is happening in Quebec is not the only matter of crucial concern to parliament, for we face the challenge of regional disparities. These questions confront us, as they did 100 years ago. All these difficulties, together with the difficulties Ontario faces, must be foremost in our minds today. I feel confident, as I am sure others do, that we will be as creative as the Fathers of Confederation were, and possibly future generations may look upon our generation as a founding one if we understand all our country's problems and come to grips with them.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to follow the erudite member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) in any debate, but I want to say that I listened with interest to his learned comments on ethylene and polyvinylchloride and the complaints he made about the economic policies which have bound this country into its present state, and I would like him to sit there and think about what administration over the years has been principally responsible for those policies about which he now complains.
Disillusionment and discontent with the terms of Confederation are not a recent phenomenon, nor have they been confined exclusively to any part of this great nation. Nova Scotia, for example, has been a province which has, in the 110 years since our nation was formed, reflected the views of the most bitter
Economic Situation
opponents of Confederation as well as the convictions of some of its most prominent advocates.
A look at contemporary history readily reveals that whenever nations begin to slide into an economic recession or encounter difficulties related to a diminution of common will and resolve, there are various regions or parts of these nations that inevitably begin expressing their feelings as to whether or not they might be better off as independent entities. Perhaps the best example of this is to be found in a nation from which we have received much of our common heritage, the United Kingdom.
When Britain was a dynamic force in world affairs with a strong, vibrant economy, a favourable balance of trade, and was a leader in technology, there was little talk of Welsh or Scottish nationalism. We are seeing now in this country, in times of adversity, the same type of situation which is prevalent in the United Kingdom where national unity is strained and where the sum of the parts of the nation appears greater than the whole. The motion, therefore, of my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), is a very timely indictment-and a very necessary one-of the government which, by its economic mismanagement, has contributed greatly to the lack of spirit and the disunity in our country.
Since this is the House of Commons and since we are the politicians in it, we all must share some of the responsibility. I know that this probably will not be a popular statement as far as some Liberals are concerned. I am sure they feel that since they have been in control of this nation's destiny for most of the past 50 years, with the authority to make most of the key decisions which have brought us to this crisis, they should be exonerated from any responsibility for it, because that is the way they think and operate, at least recently. Certainly it can never be said that in recent years the Liberal party has ever failed to place the party ahead of the country. Any suggestion that this is not the case, particularly in recent years, will not meet the test of reality.
Can you imagine, Sir, it being said of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as it was of some great Prime Ministers in our past-Sir John Thompson, for example, from Nova Scotia-that "he won't even consider whether a thing is good for the party until he is quite sure it is good for the country"?
When the present Prime Minister inherited the leadership of the Liberal party and our country, no one could deny that he acquired problems which have always characterized Canada: difficulties with transportation, problems in satisfying competing regional interests, and so on. He also inherited inflationary trends and a rather high, for those times, unemployment rate. Then, as now, relations with the United States were always an important priority for Canada on the international scene. Canadians have watched and listened to this Prime Minister since the heady days of Expo and have been assured at various times that our traditional problems were well under control. Inflation had been wrestled to the ground, unemployment had been solved, trade deficits had been overcome, the United

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
States and Canada had had a fantastic breakthrough in their relationship, and regional development was under control by virtue of the creation of the great new Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which was going to solve most of the problems of disparity in our country.
Canadians were also told that separatism was dead in this nation, and that latest piece of good news came just about a year ago. Unfortunately, all of these assurances, together with many other statements related to the economy and transportation, were and are demonstrably false, and that is part of the reason for the necessity of debating in this House the sorry state into which our nation has fallen. A little honesty in the past and fewer cliff-top orations would have served this nation much better.
The Atlantic region, like our sister province of Quebec, has suffered from long periods of chronic recession Whenever the regional disparity gap between ourselves and the rest of the country seemed to be narrowed and prosperity was on the way, some problem or other caused the region to have its growth potential blunted and its aspirations once more destroyed. As in other parts of the country, people in eastern Canada are conscious that our efforts to reach our destiny as a great nation are losing their impetus. We are all trying desperately to recapture that sense of purpose which will help us, as history unfolds, to realize our destiny as a truly great nation, and we are confident that, as the competence of governments improves, some of the misleading and untruthful predictions which have been mouthed in recent years may turn out to be true.
It was, after all, a great Liberal Prime Minister from Quebec who said that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. Well, time is running out on this century, and on a far different type of Liberal administration than the one led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for us to realize this cherished goal.
The immediate focus of attention in Canada today on the issue of national unity is on La Belle Province, and rightfully so. We in the maritimes are greatly concerned about the course of action now being taken by the Parti Quebecois, but we are, as we always have been, proud of our great sister province and of the excellence it has brought to our country in many spheres of activity: in the theatre, the arts, fashion, in sports, and particularly in making it possible for Canada to speak to the international community in two of the world's great languages.
On a lighter note, it is heartening that despite all the rampant Quebec nationalism and current talk of separation, even those zealots in the Parti Quebecois have not decided to change the name of the greatest hockey team in the world, the Montreal Canadiens, to les Quebecois de Montreal, so all is not lost.

Separatism, or independence, is not a new phenomenon in this country, nor is it peculiar to the province of Quebec. In 1867, 17 of the 18 federal candidates in Nova Scotia ran against Confederation and, what is more, they were

elected. But now no Nova Scotian premier or member of Parliament would ever come to a conference on Confederation, in this, the second century of it, with any suggestion that our province of Nova Scotia would or should ever separate, and so it will be in the future with the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
During the past century Nova Scotia has had many eloquent and able supporters of Confederation, including three prime ministers, and had the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) become the fourth Nova Scotian to become Prime Minister, our country today would be well on its way back to true unity and prosperity, because the characteristic of Nova Scotians in Confederation has always been their ability to accept adversity for the common good of the country and to work toward improving their lot and that of their nation.
That philosophy has extended from the early days of Confederation to the present time and has been echoed again and again by people like Angus L. MacDonald, that great Nova Scotian premier and federal cabinet minister, and George Nowlan, another distinguished cabinet minister and great son of our province, who pointed out in many a speech in this place that there were more than bonds of sentiment which bound this country together. He reminded us that we had a private railway and a national railway to span this continent, and a private broadcasting system and a public broadcasting system in the same way. George Nowlan reminded us as well that we could go through our national institutions, examine any one of them, and find that we have made a unique nation, one in which we could take pride instead of one for which we sometimes apologize. He admonished us to stop talking about gloom and doom and to stop taking out our livers, propping them up on our knees and examining then to see whether we had cirrhosis. His advice is as applicable now as it was then.
Our nation is a unique one, and one of which we can all be proud. Its territorial integrity can never be negotiated; however, the position we find ourselves in today is full of ironies. We see the various regions of our country chafing under a government with delusions of adequacy and under the accompanying illusion that central government planning can tinker with the economy, change policies on an ad hoc basis, and apply general measures affecting different and unique regions where specific ones are needed instead.
Jacques Parizeau, the Quebec Minister of Finance, said of his own government's economic approach that he preferred a scalpel to an axe. Our country is too fragile and too unique to be governed with the heavy-handed, uniform policies characterized by this government. We need to be molded into a force collectively, not forced into a collective mold.
In the maritimes there is no antipathy or bitterness to any other part of Canada. There is, rather, the desire not to be a burden, to help and to share in creating a great country, to develop our own resources, fisheries, forests, agriculture, mines and other industries which have shown in the past that they are viable in our own particular economic climate. We can do it, but not under the policies followed by this government, a
May 19, 1977

government which is demonstrating bankruptcy, not only in the area of policy development, but rather in an economic sense as well. It is leading our nation to the point where we are perilously close to not being able to have the financial resources to finance the great capital projects that will be needed to assure the type of sound development and construction of infrastructures and capital works projects of the type that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) had begun to put into place for this country when he was Prime Minister.
Canadians in the Atlantic Region and in Quebec remember the commitment that he had toward regional development; the steps he had begun to implement to develop the north; the first steps toward plans for a national power grid; his concept of councils of resource ministers and his determination to get rid of hyphenated Canadianism. People remember his commitment to his country. No one could ever say of the right hon. member for Prince Albert that he had any greater priorities than the welfare of his country; with him, politics came second and Canada came first.
We need a renewal of that spirit to get on with the consideration of the ends, not the argument over the jurisdictional means, toward development of our nation. Waste and incompetence in managing our country are a disgrace and a blight on our national psyche.
Consider the sorry state of some of the basic areas of administration and development under this government, such as the position in which the dredging industry now finds itself; a situation concerning which the cabinet had ample warning years ago had they chosen to act.
Consider the millions wasted in hare-brained schemes relating to employment programs-such as when the National Employment Service was disbanded and bifurcated into a Manpower and UIC system in the name of the national manpower strategy-which once more is being changed after hundreds of millions of dollars have been wasted on this administrative abortion.
Consider the monster airports which no one-particularly the industry and the people affected-wanted. Probably between Calgary and Mirabel in the last few years several hundreds of millions of dollars of unnecessary expense has been incurred with negative results as far as the public and the airline industry are concerned. Consider another example, the grandiose public works schemes in Hull which are dislocating thousands of workers and creating more problems, as usual, than they solve. Then there is the miserable and expensive failure in our prison system.
All these things and many other equally foolish projects are causing Canadians to lose heart and to lose pride in their country. They realize that the funds which were wasted, if wisely invested in the province of Quebec, as well as eastern Canada, in sound developments, in housing, in transportation, could have made a great difference in the outlook and in the prosperity of this part of our nation.
Economic Situation
Our neighbours to the south are attracting Canadian capital and Canadian talent because they are doing much better as a nation than we are. They are more competitive, more productive and, to our shame, more patriotic. In the process, in some areas, they are even becoming bilingual. Spanish is the second language now in cities like Miami, and in parts of Louisiana French is being actively taught and the use of it is being encouraged.
Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, if the government of the United States of America and its people decided to have a bilingual nation, they could do it. On the record of their performance compared to the sorry group of incompetents that are leading this country, they would probably overtake us in this field as well, before very many years had passed.
Why is our country in such a sorry state? Mr. Speaker, the main reason is that our government for some years has become obsessed and exclusively preoccupied with its own political future; far more so than with the future of the country. It is very ironic that the bastion of its power in past years is the region of Canada that is causing it the most concern and which is showing the most ingratitude today. There is something ironic in that, and it is perfectly understandable when one considers that not long ago the Prime Minister went to the province of Quebec and made savage mockery of the then Premier, Robert Bourassa.
We, as Conservatives, must bear the blame to some extent because after all we have not provided a provincial federalist party to which the people of Quebec could turn. We must therefore share the responsibility for the fact that people of Quebec, in an attempt to get rid of a corrupt and incompetent government, had to turn to an administration which, while committed to providing good and efficient government, also had a philosophic commitment to divorcing this beautiful province from the rest of us. We are not without blame either.
The remedies for Canada's problems are not simple. It took many years to bring this prosperous and happy nation to the state in which it now finds itself, and it will take some years before some of the scars can be removed.
Encouraging reduction of government powers at all levels is far more timely and more needed than transfers of power from one level of government to another. We need to restore to the various partners in Confederation, the feeling of purpose and of being masters in their own houses. We do not need any further encroachments upon the lives of our people by governments, federal, provincial, or municipal.
We need, as well as encouraging a feeling of independence and pride in our people, a re-assessment of those government programs which were supposed to have some effect in reducing regional disparities. It is becoming obvious, on the basis of independent studies by competent people and agencies, that the regional development program conceived by this government in 1969, is not working. Transfer payments have helped slow growth regions far more than has DREE acting by itself and, often, at cross purposes with other government departments. Regional development has not made much of a dent, if any, in our slow growth regions.

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
Pride in national unity is not entirely a matter of economics. Our young people, and people generally, must be persuaded to work and not to emulate the Prime Minister's philosophy of exercising their right not to work, as he once expressed it.
Instead of frittering money away on grandiose and useless projects, which in many cases do not meet with the public need or approval, we must, particularly in those areas of Canada where unemployment is highest, get on with the job of constructing power grids, opening mines, building docks, wharves, grain elevators for storage, and all the practical things that can stand us in good stead in future and help us develop our economic muscle.
Let us also, as members of this House of Commons and Senate, begin to work toward restoring a sense of respect for this place and ourselves as elected representatives of our people. Let us devote more of our energies while we are here toward the business of the country and less toward our own, and in the process consider some of the needed changes in our constitution as outlined in part by the distinguished hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe this afternoon.
Let us encourage our people by every means possible, perhaps by subsidizing travel at some periods of the year, if necessary on public transportation, to become better acquainted with our nation and the many ethnic groups in it and the many beautiful regions that many people have never seen. In this way we will not only foster pride in our country but will dispel many of the stereotyped impressions, based on lack of personal contact, that plague our country and cause tensions.
Recently in Toronto a man who had come to this country after the war from Poland approached me, and on the subject of national unity he asked, "What do you say when people make a point of saying to you that they are English or French?" While I was hesitating, not quite certain of his meaning, he broke into a broad grin and said, "I tell them 'Good for you-what part of England or France are you from?' " Then he said, "This is what is wrong with our country. People are not willing to be Canadians-they want to be one sort or another of a particular kind of Canadian."
National unity will never be truly achieved until we are proud to be Canadians first, and while not forgetting our heritage, are not working toward imposing it or flaunting it in the face of others who share origins of which they are just as proud.
Let us remember that it is not where we have been or from whence we came that is primarily important: it is where we are going, what sort of a heritage we can create, and what sort of a future we will leave for our children. National unity is terribly hard to define. Perhaps one picturesque way of trying to do so is to recall the legendary exchange that is supposed to have taken place between Hilter and Churchill some years ago, when their countries were at war. Adolph Hilter declared that "the German Reich was bound together by chains, but that the British Empire was held together only by moonbeams." To which Churchill replied, "Yes, that may be true, but have you ever tried to cut a moonbeam?"

I would prefer to think that the various parts and regions of this country will never be bound entirely together by mere physical bonds alone whether rail, road or pipeline, however important they may seem to be, but will be held together as well by common bonds that are as beautiful and as intangible and everlasting as moonbeams-the concepts, ideals and desires of all in this country to be Canadian.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before going on to a discussion of the topic before us this evening I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) for what I thought was an extremely thoughtful presentation about one aspect of the problem of Canadian unity and how it relates to the evolution of economic policy. There are certain things I strongly disagree with, but his was a very thoughtful presentation, and those who are not present this evening should read it.
I certainly think that the motion before us today on the government's responsibility for the present economic disorder in Canada and the disastrous consequences on the spirit and unity of the country, is an important one, and I congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) for introducing it. In beginning what I have to say in general support of this motion, I want to state that I recognize there are, of course, international considerations that have stimulated a good deal of economic disorder throughout the world. However, there is little doubt that the economic mismanagement of the fiscal, monetary, and commercial policies of this country has to be laid primarily at the door of the present government.
As a social democrat I am troubled at the failure of the government not only to produce more needed goods and services for Canada, but also at its general failure to redistribute income as between the lowest 20 per cent on the income scale as against the highest. The amount of unemployment, both measured and hidden, is now the highest since the depression.
Let us first look at the distribution of income. It is a sad but true fact that under this government the poorest 20 per cent of Canadians share only 4.4 per cent of Canada's economic pie, which is technically called our national income or gross national product. On the other end of our income spectrum, the wealthiest 20 per cent of Canadians share 42.2 per cent of it.
These figures have remained almost the same despite the continuous introduction of new income transfer programs and the expansion of some older ones. It is despairing that, between 1969 and 1974, the family income of the poorest 20 per cent of Canadians fell by 7 per cent. This does not say much for the old Trudeau concept of building a just society in Canada.
It is a myth for federal Liberals to be claiming that they are, through their policies, increasingly redistributing away from the rich to the poor. The fact is that these so-called transfer payments, many of which were initiated by the CCF and the NDP, have not led to a reduction in the inequality of income in
May 19, 1977

this country but rather they have held that inequality virtually steady.
There is increasing evidence that Canada's tax system is less progressive now than it was ten years ago. The poor do benefit to some extent from transfer of income through the tax system, but the rich benefit even more. This latter point has been recently documented in a study done by the National Council of Welfare report called the "Hidden Welfare System."
Professor Irwin Gillespie's studies at Carleton University, and Gillespie is an acknowledged authority on how incomes are distributed in Canada, have pointed out that the total public sector does restribute income, but its redistribution is away from the middle and upper middle classes to both extremes of the income scale, to the poorest and the richest.
The net gains to the poor are twice as large as the gains to the upper middle classes, but the gains to a family in the richest income class are largest of all, some three times larger than the gains to the poorest family. In short, as Gillespie shows, the increasing contribution of middle and upper middle income Canadians generates the major gains to rich Canadians; each rich family gained three times more than each poor family and six times more than each middle income family.
It is distressing to realize that because of the loopholes allowed to the rich by this government, and because of the larger negative and regressive impact of federal and provincial sales taxes, as well as property taxes on the poor and low income earners, I repeat it is distressing to realize that the increase of transfer payments and higher taxes have left the poor in this country proportionately worse off in the middle of the 1970's than they were at the end of the 1960's.
It is equally distressing, if not more so, to see clear cut evidence, which the media in this country rarely focuses on, that the relative improvement of the rich has, for the most part, been at the expense of the middle class. Something is obviously wrong with the economic system and the management of it by this government.
Two of the serious implications of what I am saying about distribution of income refer to two groups in our society. The first is the one parent family headed by women. The second is the poor kids that exist in Canada. Let us discuss the question of one parent families headed by women.
In 1974, according to the last official statistics I have seen,
300,000	Canadian families had only one parent. In 261,230 of them, the parent is the mother. This has occurred of course because of the fivefold increase in divorces between 1964 and 1974, as well as because of desertion and deaths. Between 1966 and 1971, the number of single parent families increased at three times the rate of two parent families. The pressures on the women who are heads of these families is almost unbelievable, since studies show that poverty affects 53 per cent of all one parent families.
These pressures particularly affect women on their own. In 1973 the survey of consumer finances discovered that 59.6 per cent of single parent women lived in poverty. This compares
Economic Situation
with a national average of 12.7 per cent of all families and only 14.1 per cent for single parent males. The reason is obvious. Single men can get a job far more easily than single women, who can seldom get a job paying enough to support their children. Instead, they are forced onto welfare.
In 1974 almost 40 per cent of all Canadian women were working. They made up over 34 per cent of the Canadian labour force. Their earnings, though based on a 1973 Statistics Canada figure, were such that 45.9 per cent of all women heads of families earned less than $2.50 per hour. At the same time, only 11.2 per cent of male family heads earned that little. Of the over 631,000 children of single parent families in Canada, approximately 143,000 are pre-schoolers. Yet in 1974 there were only 50,000 daycare places available in Canada. Now what about the poor children?
The "Poor Kids" report by the National Council of Welfare on children in poverty in Canada, published in March, 1975, showed that there are more than one and a half million poor children in Canada.
I remember my leader asking me to do a short resume on behalf of our party over the CBC on this. I received ten letters saying it was not true. I sent each of those people who corresponded with me a copy of the report. Except for one person, each of them wrote back saying that they were shocked to see a verification of the poverty in that report.
As the report revealed, poor children are more likely than middle class children to be born prematurely, to be less fit, to have lower IQ ratings, and to underachieve in the school system. It goes without saying that poor children are less well represented in court. One of the striking things about this study is that it reveals that 60 per cent of all poor children in Canada live in Ontario or Quebec.
Let us look at unemployment under this government. Of course we know this is one of our most serious problems. If you count the official figure, which is over 900,000, along with the unofficial figure for the number of hidden unemployed, sometimes referred to as "discouraged workers" you arrive at a figure which is closer to 1,200,000. There is little doubt that with a growth rate in the economy projected at between 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent this year, the national unemployment rate this winter will be as high as 8.5 per cent or 9 per cent. Indeed, it will be much higher still except for a factor referred to as a decline in the participation rate in the labour force, which occurs when there are no jobs available in the economy. In such a situation the percentage of people working and looking for work automatically goes down. This is very true of the Atlantic region. Thus, the official unemployment rate as put out by Statistics Canada misstates the under-utilization of human beings in our economy.
Not only are we failing to produce many billions of dollars worth of needed goods and services which could have been produced had the unemployment rate been, say, 4 per cent, but one must also take into account the loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in the form of taxation of governments at all

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
levels, plus the enormous unemployment insurance pay-outs which are presently necessary. The high unemployment is one of the major reasons why the budgetary deficit is so great.
I know that at the present time there is an attempt being made to rationalize the situation in many parts of the establishment by saying that unemployment is not as hard on people as it was in the thirties. This is little comfort to people who have to bring up families and maintain a standard of living in the seventies. It is said that, given the present rates of unemployment insurance benefits and other social programs, it is mainly the housewives, the young adults and people over 55 who are affected, not primary breadwinners. In other words, it is claimed that the composition of the unemployed has changed and that this makes a significant difference. To my mind, when government spokesmen use an argument of this kind- I recall the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) and the former minister of manpower and immigration, as well as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), resorting to it-it is no more than an attempt to rationalize a serious situation. None of us in this House would judge our standard of living, except that we are now getting large salaries, on any other basis but on family income. In other words, if you were a lawyer before you came here you would be judging your standard of living on the income you received as a lawyer and on the income which might be coming from other members of the family. And if this goes for that profession, what must it be like for the average Canadian?
The point I am trying to make is that we have to judge the seriousness of the unemployment among women, housewives, young adults and so on, by what it does to family incomes, rather than using the rationalization that it is not such a serious problem because it falls on the categories of people I have mentioned. We recall what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said on one occasion about the changes in eligibility for unemployment insurance. It might have been a slip of the tongue, but it was very significant nevertheless. He said it was only housewives and "kids" who would be affected.
We know that unemployment among our youth is very serious, and attention has been called to it in a special way by figures recently released by Statistics Canada. Although I am supporting this motion put forward by the official opposition I was startled to read recently in the Ottawa Citizen about a dialogue which was supposed to have taken place between the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and a student at Medicine Hat, Alberta, on this question of student unemployment. The student was asking the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, according to this article, about a guaranteed income proposal he had endorsed during the leadership race last year. The Leader of the Official Opposition told the student he no longer favoured the proposal because recent abuses of unemployment insurance had convinced him it might prove too strong a disincentive to work. According to this report, he added, "The natural instinct to work is not as strong among young Canadians as I had thought." That is not exactly a new view. Nor is it supported by the facts.

While three out of every eight unemployment insurance recipients are under the age of 25, fully half of Canada's unemployed are in that age bracket. As beneficiaries of jobless pay, young people are actually under-represented. There is nothing mysterious about that. It is just that even the eight weeks of steady work needed to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits are hard to come by when job seekers outnumber jobs by almost 20 to one.
In the past two years the number of unemployed young people has grown from 258,000 to 387,000-from 9.6 per cent of those between 15 and 54 years of age in the labour force to a figure of 14 per cent. Some, including the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration, have tried to pin the blame on the education system. The hon. gentleman told a recent conference:
It is time for us in Canada to reorient our educational systems so that young people get the education and training which will ensure them employment.
Unfortunately the minister failed to explain what kind of education and training would enable the 778,000 then unemployed to fit into the 41,000 jobs which were then vacant.
