speechtext:
In conclusion I should like to make a few comments on the issue of national unity. I thought I would have a little more time to spend on that question.
To the extent that the performance, or lack of performance, of the economy has intensified the Quebec separatist movement, the present government must be held responsible for the unemployment rate of some 10 per cent which exists in that province. At least 40 per cent of the young people in Quebec are suffering the effects of unemployment generated in large part by the failure of the federal government's economic policy. It cannot be blamed on the Parti Quebecois.
The government has certainly mismanaged the national economy and we, in the Atlantic region, together with our fellow citizens in Quebec, share the legacy, as I have already noted, in the form of extraordinarily high unemployment. It is little wonder that a tenured, separatist, professional elite at the University of Montreal and other universities in the province, as well as teachers at high school level, find willing ears among young Quebec students as they advocate their separatist ideas. After all, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) comes from that province, and he was telling us last year that separatism was dead. Some death! No wonder we are in trouble as a nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to speak the full 20 minutes, but the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) also has to get in his speech tonight so I
May 19, 1977

will keep my remarks to not more than ten minutes to give him at least a few minutes in which to say a few words.
I should like to congratulate the mover of this motion who, I am sorry, is not here at this point, on the speech he made today. It was a speech that contained a great deal of moderation and thought. Many other speeches have been made along the same line, and in general I think we have been looking for solutions to the problems confronting us.
At a time when the economy has been growing at the rate of 3 to 4 per cent over the last eight or ten years as opposed to growth of perhaps 2 per cent over the last century, when we are fourth or fifth lowest in terms of rate of inflation among OECD countries, when we have created by far the largest number of jobs of any country among OECD countries in the last five to six years, and when we weathered best the recession compared with other OECD countries, it seems strange that there should be such concern and malaise in the country today.
Under normal circumstances, Mr. Speaker, our achievements might be considered a roaring success, but these are not normal circumstances. These are not normal times but very complex times. In order to solve our problems we must look at the future very differently from the way we looked ahead in former times. We must find different solutions because the problems are different.
Most of us in this House grew up and were educated under a regime which told us there were no such things as shortages- if only we could let ourselves go we could have everything in Canada. We were told we had all the resources necessary, and in such great abundance around us that we could consume, consume, consume. That has been the modus vivendi of our society. Then in the past three or four years a very important change came about. Instead of the notion of cheap and abundant energy, we have now reached a point where we are facing shortages of energy. All of a sudden we have a totally new concept; instead of the concept of abundance we have the concept of shortage.
In the last few days we had a report published by the workshop on alternate energy sources which told us that as early as 1985 the world will experience a very serious shortage of oil. By the end of the century this shortage will be such that we will probably have to convert to other energy supplies, and automobiles in their present form will no longer exist. This is a major problem which will require some very serious thought and radical change.
We are also told that in the next 15 years Canada will need $180 billion for energy capital in today's dollars. This means that every family unit in the country will be required to pay out something like $30,000, almost the equivalent of the cost of a home in today's dollars. Last week we had a magnificent report by Mr. Justice Berger which told us about the problems of the north, both environmental and social, which this kind of energy development could cause. We have been told by the President of the United States, and by our own energy minister, that we must change our ways, that we must learn to conserve, that we must move away from a consumption type
Economic Situation
economy. We must embark upon a wholly new lifestyle. As I say, these are not the times we have known in the past.
Another problem facing us is inflation. Inflation is worldwide and not confined to Canada or to one or two countries here and there. With almost no exception there seems to be a basic inflation rate of 5 per cent no matter what one does. This 5 per cent basic inflation rate was discussed at the economic summit and seems to be an insuperable problem.
Unemployment is also a word-wide problem. Even with a 3 to 4 per cent growth rate there is massive unemployment, not just in Canada but all over the industrial world. Despite more than a 20 per cent increase in jobs in this country between 1971 and 1975, twice the rate of any other country in the OECD group, we have serious unemployment in Canada. Consumer demand is growing at a rate of 5 to 6 per cent a year, despite the energy shortage. In the last few months $2.4 billion was pumped into the economy in terms of demand money. Despite the last budget and indexing, we still have massive unemployment.
Unemployment is a structural problem, not a problem which can be solved by increasing money supply and consumer demand. If you have a 4.6 per cent unemployment rate in Alberta but a 17.4 per cent unemployment rate in Newfoundland and you increase consumer demand, this will mean that most of the benefit will go to Alberta with only a slight lowering of the unemployment rate in Newfoundland. In other words, it is a structural problem which requires a structural answer.
I should like to deal with the regional approach because I think this is the direction in which we should go. For example, I am pleased at the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to allow the act to function differently in the Atlantic provinces from the way the act functions in Toronto.
Young people and women who enter the labour force also face a serious employment problem. During the 1950's about
60,000	young people were leaving schools, universities and so on and entering the labour market annually. Today this figure is around 250,000 a year and is rising, and we are told that the situation will not improve until well into the 1990's. How can we solve this kind of problem?
The thing that bothers me a great deal about the situation is that we are virtually setting up two classes of Canadians. One class of Canadian is employed in the work force permanently. The other class, which I think consists mostly of young people, may very well never be part of the work force. I do not think we can solve this problem by increasing demand or even by government projects. Rather we must look at the total work force and at the amount of work that can gainfully be done, and then somewhere along the line there must be a concept of work sharing, some way in which young people can plug into the labour market and older people can retire earlier. We have to look at new ideas to solve this problem.
In conclusion, these are unique times. I would love to develop that notion, but these are very, very different times,

May 19, 1977
Economic Situation
and the solutions are not going to be the standard ones we hear talked about in this House. We must move in new directions and do a lot of new thinking before we come to a successful solution to the problems we have. We must change our lifestyle significantly in the next four or five years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) for giving up some of his time to allow me to have a word or two at the end of this important debate today. I am pleased and proud to have the opportunity to be the closing speaker in this debate because I think it is an important one. The parliament of Canada must get involved in an understanding and a discussion of the issues, which have to be the most important issues that have faced Canada since Confederation.
I have been alarmed and distressed, since the election of Mr. Levesque in the province of Quebec, that this parliament has been moribund in not dealing or discussing with any sort of depth the real issues which are facing the nation. If we do not start to face them in the federal parliament of Canada, we will lead to the destruction of the nation we all cherish so much. The party which 1 have the honour of representing today has done a major service in introducing a motion which asks parliamentarians to look at issues which are important in Canada today. 1 am referring mainly to the important issue of separation. I am sorry the motion today was not dealt with in a more direct manner.
What has been the fundamental relationship between the development of separatism in the province of Quebec and the operation of the economic policy of this nation as a whole? Historically you will not find any examples where separatism in a country has risen except in response to a very strong differentiation in levels of economic performance.
If you look at the evolution issue in Great Britain today, the problem areas for the British are Scotland and Wales. There have been major differences in levels of economic performance there. If you look at France, Brittany is the area which has been concerned about the operation of the country as a whole. It has been an area of deprivation. The areas where federalism has really worked are areas where there have not been major differentiations in levels of economic performance. If you look at Canada and analyse the economic performance in the province of Quebec, as related to economic performance in other areas of this country, the reality is that the province of Quebec has had a much poorer economic performance than the rest of the country as a whole.
In the province of Quebec the level of unemployment has been consistently high and the rate of investment has been consistently low. The question one has to ask is: why? The national government has the responsibility for economic performance. It has the responsibility for doing something about the differentiation in regional rates of development. It has failed. The issue is very important and must be made clear to the people of the province of Quebec. They have been given a song by the premier of Quebec that they can have political independence and the same standard of living which they have at the present time. It is a song which is very hard to resist. To

the terrible criticism of all of us in the Parliament of Canada, it is going unanswered.
The program being offered by the premier of Quebec is going to be irresistible to many of the people in that province because it is based on some very real facts. The people who happen to be members of parliament in Canada at this time will be looked on by their children and grandchildren as having not even responded to these issues. If anyone canvasses around Canada, they will find out that the respect the people of Canada have for their members of parliament has gone down. The reason is very clear. We are not living up to our responsibilities. We are not debating the real issues in the House of Commons of Canada today. We are not raising the questions about which the people of Canada care. They care about keeping this country together. They want this country kept together, and we do not talk about it here. We do not debate it here.
We had an opportunity today to come to grips with this issue. I have great respect for the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell). He did not direct himself to this issue. He spoke about the west, in a debate which ought to be on whether or not this country is going to stay together. He spoke about tariffs. That is not the issue. The issue is: why has not the federal Government of Canada been able to provide for the people of Quebec an economic opportunity equivalent to that enjoyed by the rest of the people of Canada?

speechtext: The statistics are very clear. They show the people of the province of Quebec have been faced with an unemployment rate which has been consistently 20 per cent higher than the rest of Canada. Why is that so when they have the resource base they possess? To mention the Atlantic provinces is irrelevant. It is also unimportant in this context if you look at the resource base in those areas. The important issue to the people of the province of Quebec is whether they are going to stay in Confederation. I do not care whether you are Liberal, Conservative, NDP or Creditiste. That is irrelevant to me. I would like to see this country stay together. That is what I care about.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY FOR "ECONOMIC DISORDER"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I do not care about those other things. The people of Quebec know their economic performance has been low. It is our responsibility to have an important debate to show them, if they separate and if they vote for Mr. Levesque, that their performance will not be improved. They have to be shown that the reasons for their low economic performance are not endemic to Confederation.
If they decide to go with Mr. Levesque in the province of Quebec, which is a market of six million people instead of 22 million people, with a concern about investment being slowed down because of uncertainty, and a concern about nationalization of asbestos, their standard of living is going to be much less than if they stay within Confederation. Nobody in this
May 19, 1977

parliament or in this country is telling the people of Quebec that story. As federal politicians we are going to find out, because we did not tell them that story-

CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST THAT FINAL GAMES OF WORLD HOCKEY LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP BE TELEVISED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the greatest pleasure I would have allowed the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) some of my time tonight because I will not need seven minutes. I will try to follow on the same theme as the hon. member for Don Valley has raised this evening, which is Canadian unity.
The reason I am on my feet tonight is in regard to the problems we are facing in Canada with hundreds of thousands of people requesting that the WHL hockey finals be televised. We have had very little success with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in resolving this problem until today. The hockey finals could be a great step toward Canadian unity. This matter has nothing to do with French, English, or anything else. People in Quebec, in Manitoba, and in the rest of Canada want to see the hockey finals. We have been running into a blank wall, and the matter has now reached the floor of the House of Commons. It has been brought up time and time again over the last number of weeks, and today it took three members of parliament to raise this issue before we could get any action on why CBC will not televise the WHL finals. One of the reasons given is that they show too much sport. It is said that the WHA games are not on the same level as those of the NHL. I do not agree. Today the WHA is on the same level as the NHL. Since hundreds of thousands of people are demanding the televising of this particular hockey final, the least the CBC can do is comply with their wishes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST THAT FINAL GAMES OF WORLD HOCKEY LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP BE TELEVISED
speechtext: This government does not care.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST THAT FINAL GAMES OF WORLD HOCKEY LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP BE TELEVISED
speechtext:
As I said earlier, three members of parliament raised the question in the House, I being one of them, but we got absolutely no answers from the three ministers we questioned. I pursued the question this afternoon in the Stand-
Adjournment Debate
ing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. The President of the CBC, Mr. A. Johnston, was there. Since I raised this question in committee this afternoon, several things have happened. I received three telephone calls from the CBC this evening. Apparently they are prepared to show a couple of these final games live. I am repeating what I have been told by CBC officials. Incidentally, I am pleased to note the presence in the House of the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) who answers for the CBC. I hope he will confirm what the CBC liaison officer in the House of Commons told me this evening. I am told that the fifth game can be shown live, if that game can be scheduled for the afternoon.
If the WHA cannot schedule that game for the afternoon, the CBC will tape the game and show it after the news on Sunday night. The CBC has also informed me that the sixth game can be taped and shown on Tuesday night, May 24, after the late night news. That tapes game will also be shown in Quebec.
The CBC has presented the WHA with an alternative proposal. The CBC told the WHA that if Tuesday's game could be moved to Thursday, the CBC would be able to cover that game live, and broadcast it live in Manitoba and Quebec, and I presume right across Canada. The CBC also says that, if a seventh game is necessary, if it is played on the afternoon of Saturday, May 28, it could be televised live on the English and French networks.
Apparently we have made progress since this afternoon as a result of previous representations in the House, letters, telephone calls and so on. I hope the minister will confirm what I have just placed on record with regard to the CBC's providing coverage of the WHA finals.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST THAT FINAL GAMES OF WORLD HOCKEY LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP BE TELEVISED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member who reminds me of a barnyard cock who firmly believes the sun rises every day because he crows.
The hon. member raised this question today in the House, and he also raised it in committee this afternoon. But the matter was raised by others long before the hon. member showed any interest in it. It was raised by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos), and by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). The fact is that such interventions in relation to this question did not begin this afternoon. They began last week. I myself called the parliamentary liaison officer to the CBC on Friday, and there have been continuing contacts between my office and the CBC with respect to this issue for several days. The results which the hon. member has proudly proclaimed as coming from his interventions are actually the results of interventions made by members on this side of the House long before he showed any interest in the matter.
The point I would like to make is that in terms of the intervention of ministers in relation to these matters it is not the Secretary of State who has the power to intervene with the CBC or to direct it to do this or that in terms of its internal management, its day-to-day decisions or its programming. The

May 19, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Secretary of State is a link between hon. members of this House and the CBC, and as such 1 do bring to the attention of the CBC the complaints which are presented to me by hon. members of this House and the concerns which they express. That is what I have done in this case, and I am very happy to be able to indicate to the House that the interventions which
were made by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos) and my colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), have been successful.
